competition: St. Petersburg Mathematical Olympiad (oldest grade, final round)

problems.problem: The base of a pyramid of volume $V$ is a trapezoid with bases $m$ and $n$. A plane cuts off from it a pyramid of volume $U$, and the cross-section is again a trapezoid, with bases $m_1$ and $n_1$. Prove that $$\frac{U}{V}=\frac{(m_1+n_1)m_1n_1}{(m+n)mn}.$$

A school teaches $2n$ subjects. All pupils get only marks 4 and 5, and no two pupils have identical marks in all subjects. For no two pupils can one say that one of them does at least as well as the other in every subject. Prove that the number of pupils in the school does not exceed $\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!\,n!}$.
Find the least value of the expression $(a^2+x^2)/x$, where $a>0$ is a constant and $x>0$ is a variable.

Let $f(x)=x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\ldots+a_n$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients, and let $p$ be a rational root of it. Prove that $p$ is an integer and that $f(m)$ is divisible by $p-m$ for every integer $m$.
Prove that $\tan 20^\circ-\tan 40^\circ+\tan 80^\circ=3\sqrt{3}$.

Each face of a cube is covered with two right triangles, one white and one black. Prove that there exist only two essentially different ways of covering (that is, ways that cannot be carried into each other by rotations of the cube) such that at each vertex the sum of the white angles meeting there equals the sum of the black angles.

A snail crawls on a table at constant speed. Every 15 minutes it turns through $90^\circ$, and between turns it crawls along a straight line. Prove that it can return to its starting point only after a whole number of hours.
A quadrilateral is inscribed in a unit square, with a vertex on each side of the square. Prove that one of its sides has length at least $1/\sqrt{2}$.
The polynomial $x^{kn}+a_1x^{k(n-1)}+a_2x^{k(n-2)}+\ldots+a_{n-1}x^k+a_n$ is divisible by $x-1$. Prove that it is divisible by $x^k-1$.
Find the sum $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}k^2$.
Rationalize the denominator of $$\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{a}+\sqrt[3]{b}+\sqrt[3]{c}}.$$

Two segments are given on the two sides of an angle. A point $O$ inside the angle is joined to the endpoints of these segments, and the sum of the areas of the two triangles so obtained equals $S$. Find the locus of points $M$ for which the analogous sum of areas equals $S$.

A polyhedron is given. The number of sides of each of its faces except one is divisible by a given natural number $n>1$. Prove that the faces of this polyhedron cannot be coloured in two colours so that adjacent faces have different colours.
Solve in natural numbers the equation $$1-\cfrac{1}{2+\cfrac{1}{3+\cfrac{1}{4+\cfrac{1}{\ldots+\cfrac{1}{n}}}}}=\cfrac{1}{x_1+\cfrac{1}{x_2+\cfrac{1}{x_3+\cfrac{1}{\ldots+\cfrac{1}{x_n}}}}}.$$

A convex polygon of area greater than $1/2$ is placed inside a $1\times 1$ square. Prove that the polygon has a chord of length greater than $1/2$ parallel to any side of the square chosen in advance.
Prove that a disc of radius $2$ can be completely covered by seven discs of radius $1$, but a disc of larger radius cannot.
Nine polygons, each of area $1$, are placed in a square of area $5$. Prove that some two of them have an intersection of area at least $1/9$.

A sphere is divided into three regions, each painted in its own colour, and the boundaries of the regions are painted in both colours. Prove that there is a diameter whose endpoints have the same colour.
Prove that a number written only with zeros and ones, with at least two ones, cannot be a perfect square.
Prove that from any $k$ integers one can choose several whose sum is divisible by $k$.
Solve the equation $(x^{n(n-1)/2}-x^{[n/2]})/(x-1)=0$.

Infinite sequences whose terms are from the numbers $1,2,\ldots,n$ are considered. Two terms of two sequences are called identical if they are equal and have the same index. How many sequences can be formed so that any two of them have exactly $k$ identical terms?
Prove that if two equations with integer coefficients $$X^2+p_1X+q_1=0,\qquad X^2+p_2X+q_2=0$$ have a common non-integer root, then $p_1=p_2$ and $q_1=q_2$.
A trihedral angle and a point $A$ on one of its edges are given. Points $B$ and $C$ slide along its two other edges. Find the locus of the centroids of the triangles $ABC$.

Prove that the equation $A_1x_1+A_2x_2+\ldots+A_nx_n=B$ cannot be satisfied by more than half of all the tuples $(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ in which each $x_i$ equals $0$ or $1$, provided that not all of the numbers $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n,B$ are zero.

A plane angle $\alpha$ of a polyhedron is said to be adjacent to an edge if this edge is a side of the angle $\alpha$. Prove that every triangular pyramid has an edge to which only acute angles are adjacent.

Prove that for any $k$ infinite sequences of natural numbers $$\begin{array}{llll} x^1_1, & x^1_2, & x^1_3, & \ldots\\ x^2_1, & x^2_2, & x^2_3, & \ldots\\ \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots\\ x^k_1, & x^k_2, & x^k_3, & \ldots \end{array}$$ there exist indices $p$ and $q$ such that $x^i_p\geqslant x^i_q$ for every $1\leqslant i\leqslant k$.
Prove that one cannot place $10$ equal squares in the plane so that no square overlaps the interior of another and one of the squares touches all the others.
Find the first $1963$ digits after the decimal point in the decimal expansion of $(\sqrt{26}+5)^{1963}$.
How should a matchbox be placed in space so that its projection onto a plane has the largest area?
Five discs are given in the plane, every two of which intersect. Prove that some three of them have a common point.

A natural number $a$ is divisible by $1,2,3,\ldots,9$. Prove that if $2a$ is represented as a sum of several summands, each equal to one of $1,2,3,\ldots,9$, then some of these summands add up to $a$.
Four positive numbers are given such that the sum of any three of them is greater than the fourth. Prove that there exists a triangular pyramid whose faces have these numbers as their areas.
Solve in integers the equation $$x^4-2y^4-4z^4-8t^4=0.$$
Prove that a closed broken line of length $1$ lying in the plane can be covered by a disc of radius $1/4$.
Does there exist a triangle whose side lengths, altitudes and angle bisectors all have integer lengths?
For which $n$ is $2^n+1$ a nontrivial power of a natural number?
Squared paper is given. Two parallel lines are drawn through two lattice points. Prove that the closed strip formed contains infinitely many lattice points.
A convex $N$-gon $P$ lies inside a unit square. Prove that there are three vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ of the $N$-gon $P$ such that $S(ABC)\leqslant 100/N^2$.
A coordinate system is given in the plane. Let $N$ be the number of points $(x,y)$ with integer coordinates satisfying $x^2+y^2<n^2$, where $n$ is an integer. Prove that $N\geqslant 3(n-1)^2$.

A circle of unit radius and four points on it are given. Through every two neighbouring points a circle of unit radius is drawn. Prove that the four other intersection points of consecutive circles lie on one circle.

Let $\alpha_n$ be the exponent of $2$ in the prime factorization of $n$. Put $S_n=\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\ldots+\alpha_n$. Prove that in the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \ldots, S_{2^n-1}$ the numbers of even and of odd terms differ by one.
Two points $A$ and $B$ and a line $L$ are given in the plane. Find a point $E$ on the line $L$ such that $AE+BE=d$, where $d$ is a given number.

Let $S$ be a set of natural numbers less than a given prime $P$ such that whenever the numbers $A$ and $B$ belong to the set, so do the remainders of $AB$, $A$ and $B$ upon division by $P$. Prove that if $S$ contains at least two numbers, then the sum of the numbers in $S$ is divisible by $P$.

The vertices of two acute-angled triangles lie on the two different pairs of opposite sides of a unit square. Prove that the area of their common part is at most four times the product of the areas of the triangles.

A collection of natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ is given, some of which may be equal. Denote by $f_k$ the number of numbers of the collection that are not less than $k$. Prove that $f_1+f_2+\ldots=a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n$.
A unit square is covered by $n$ figures so that each of its points belongs to at least $q$ figures. Prove that at least one figure has area not less than $q/n$.
Suppose all real numbers are split into two groups. Prove that for every $k>0$ there are three numbers $a<b<c$ from the same group such that $(c-b)/(b-a)=k$.
Place in an equilateral triangle with unit side a triangle with given angles so that it has the largest possible area.

There are $N$ coiners. Some of them make only counterfeit coins, the others only genuine ones. The weight of a counterfeit coin differs from that of a genuine one. There is a balance with a complete set of weights and one coin known to be genuine. One may take as many coins as one likes from each coiner. How can all the counterfeiters be identified with three weighings?
Solve in integers the equation $$6xy-4x+9y-366=0.$$
Find the sum $$\frac{1}{\cos\alpha\cos 2\alpha}+\frac{1}{\cos 2\alpha\cos 3\alpha}+\ldots+\frac{1}{\cos(n-1)\alpha\cos n\alpha}.$$

Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ and $B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n$ be two permutations of the numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, n$. Prove that for even $n$ some two of the numbers $A_1+B_1, A_2+B_2, \ldots, A_n+B_n$ leave the same remainder upon division by $n$.
Prove the inequality $$(a+b)^n\leqslant 2^{n-1}(a^n+b^n),$$ where $a$ and $b$ are non-negative numbers.
A $12\times 12\times 12$ cube is cut by planes parallel to its faces into unit cubes. Into how many parts is the cube divided if a cross-section in the form of a regular hexagon is made in it?

Three circles are given. Find a point in the plane such that the right-hand tangents drawn from it to the circles form equal angles with one another.

Non-negative integers are written in the cells of an $n\times n$ table, and if some cell contains a zero, then the sum of all numbers standing in the same row or in the same column as this cell is at least $n$. Prove that the sum of the numbers in the table is at least $n/2$.
Positive numbers $a, b, c, x, y, z$ satisfy $a<b<c$; $a\leqslant x<y<z\leqslant c$; $abc=xyz$; $a+b+c=x+y+z$. Prove that $a=x$, $b=y$, $c=z$.
Among all polynomials of the form $x^2+ax+b$, find the one whose maximum absolute value on the segment $[-1;1]$ is minimal.
Prove that the area of a square placed inside a triangle does not exceed half the area of the triangle.
A figure of area less than $1$ is given on the squared plane. Prove that this figure can be translated so that no lattice point lies inside it.
Find the locus of the centres of the equilateral triangles circumscribed about a given triangle.
Cut out of a given rectangle a rhombus of the largest area.
How many integer solutions does the equation $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=\sqrt{1960}$ have?
Prove that the plane can be coloured with eleven colours so that the distance between any two points of the same colour is different from $1966$ metres.
There are $k$ colours. In how many ways can the sides of a given regular $n$-gon be coloured so that adjacent sides have different colours (the polygon may not be rotated)?

For which $\varepsilon$ can a segment of length $2a$ be divided into $n$ segments, each of length at most $a$, so that no segment whose length differs from $a$ by less than $\varepsilon$ can be composed of them?
Find all complex solutions of the system of equations $$\begin{cases} x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_n=n\\ x_1^2+x_2^2+\ldots+x_n^2=n\\ \ldots\\ x_1^n+x_2^n+\ldots+x_n^n=n. \end{cases}$$
$m$ and $n$ are natural numbers, and $m$ is odd. Prove that the numbers $2^n+1$ and $2^m-1$ are coprime.
Let $T_n$ be the area of the largest $n$-gon contained in a given convex $k$-gon (for $3<n<k$). Prove that $T_{n-1}+T_{n+1}\leqslant 2T_n$ for every $n<k$.
From the numbers $1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots, 2n$, $[(2n-2)/3]$ numbers are deleted. Prove that among the remaining numbers there are two, one of which is twice the other.

A decomposition of a square is a partition of it into finitely many rectangles whose sides are parallel to the sides of the square. A decomposition is called primitive if it is not a subdivision of a coarser decomposition. For which $n$ does a primitive decomposition of a square into $n$ rectangles exist?

$n$ points in general position are given in the plane. Some of them are joined by segments so that from each point one can get to any other in a unique way. Prove that there are $n^{n-2}$ such ways of joining them.

An $n$-gon with sides $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ is inscribed in a circle so that the centre of the circle lies inside the $n$-gon. Prove that this circle can be covered by $n$ discs of radii $na_1/6, na_2/6, \ldots, na_n/6$.
Consecutive odd numbers $p$ and $q$ are given. Prove that $p^q+q^p$ is divisible by $p+q$.

A point $M$ lies inside an equilateral triangle $ABC$, and $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$ are its projections onto the sides $BC$, $AC$, $AB$ respectively. Prove that $$AB_1\cdot BC_1+BC_1\cdot CA_1+CA_1\cdot AB_1=AC_1\cdot BA_1+BA_1\cdot CB_1+CB_1\cdot AC_1.$$

A sequence of $k$ numbers is given. It is allowed to replace any number by the sum of the numbers standing to its right. Prove that if this operation is performed sufficiently many times, then some sequence will occur twice in a row.

Let $a_1\geqslant a_2\geqslant\ldots\geqslant a_n\geqslant 0$, and let $B$ be the largest of the numbers $|b_1|, |b_1+b_2|, \ldots, |b_1+b_2+\ldots+b_n|$. Prove that $|a_1b_1+a_2b_2+\ldots+a_nb_n|\leqslant Ba_1$.
A man is lost in a forest that has the shape of a convex polygon of area $1\ \text{km}^2$. Prove that he can always get out of the forest by walking a path shorter than $2507$ metres.
Prove that there exists a finite set of points in the plane such that for each point of the set there are at least one hundred points of the set equidistant from it.

Find on squared paper a figure consisting of the smallest number of cells with the following property: if two players play noughts and crosses on the cells of this figure, then the first player can always be the first to put three crosses in a row.

Two circles intersect at a point $A$; $AB$ and $AC$ are chords of them, each of which is at the same time tangent to the other circle at $A$. Denote the second intersection point of the circles by $D$. Prove that $|AB|^2/|AC|^2=|BD|/|CD|$.
Two polynomials with real coefficients take integer values at exactly the same points. Prove that either their sum or their difference is a constant.

A point is taken on each side of a triangle, and these points are joined by segments. This produces four small triangles. It is known that the perimeters of all these triangles are equal. Prove that the chosen points are the midpoints of the sides.
There are $18$ people in a company. Prove that among them there are four people who pairwise do not know each other or four people who pairwise know each other.

Non-negative numbers are written in an $N\times N$ square table so that their sum in every row, as well as in every column, equals $1$. Prove that one can choose $N$ positive numbers in this table no two of which are in the same row or in the same column.
A sequence $0<a_0<a_1<a_2<\ldots<a_{25}<a_{26}$ is given such that $a_n=2\sqrt{a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}^4}$ for $0<n\leqslant 26$. Prove that $a_0<7\cdot 10^{-8}$.
Triangles $ABC$, $A_1B_1C_1$, $A_2B_2C_2$ with areas $S$, $S_1$, $S_2$ satisfy $AB=A_1B_1+A_2B_2$, $BC=B_1C_1+B_2C_2$, $AC=A_1C_1+A_2C_2$. Prove that $S\geqslant 4\sqrt{S_1S_2}$.
How many solutions does the system of equations $$\begin{cases}\cos x_1=x_2,\\ \cos x_2=x_3,\\ \ldots\\ \cos x_n=x_1\end{cases}$$ have?
$ABC$ and $A_1B_1C_1$ are equilateral triangles of the same orientation, $AA_1=a$, $BB_1=b$, and the angle between $AA_1$ and $BB_1$ equals $\alpha$. Find $CC_1$.

An infinite sheet of squared paper is coloured with $10$ colours so that each cell is coloured in one colour and all the colours are used. Two colours are called neighbouring if there are two cells with a common side coloured in these colours. What is the least possible number of pairs of neighbouring colours?
Prove that a regular tetrahedron cannot be cut into several pairwise different regular tetrahedra.
$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are positive numbers and $k$ is a natural number. Prove that $$(\sqrt{2}-1)(a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n)\leqslant\sqrt[k]{a_1^k\cdot 2+a_2^k\cdot 2^2+\ldots+a_n^k\cdot 2^n}.$$
Two chords $AB$ and $AC$ are drawn in a circle. From the midpoint $M$ of the arc $BAC$ a perpendicular is dropped to the longer of the chords. Prove that its foot bisects the broken line $BAC$.

$N$ points are given on a circle. Two players play a game: they move a pencil from one point to another along the segment joining these points. The moves are made in turn, and it is forbidden to draw the same segment twice. The player who cannot move loses. Prove that the first player wins with correct play.
$M$ points are given in the plane, not all on one line. Prove that one can find at least $(M-1)(M-2)/2$ triangles with vertices at these points.
$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_p$ are real numbers, $M$ is the largest of them and $m$ is the smallest. Prove that $$(p-1)(M-m)\leqslant\sum_{i<j}|a_i-a_j|\leqslant p^2\,\frac{M-m}{4}.$$
Prove that the sum of the distances from a point inside a tetrahedron to its vertices is less than its perimeter.
Find an integer $n$ such that the decimal representation of the number $5^n$ contains at least $1968$ consecutive zeros.

A convex polyhedron is given in each vertex of which three faces meet. Each face is painted in one of four colours, and faces with a common edge have different colours. Prove that the number of faces of the first colour having an odd number of sides has the same parity as the number of faces of the second colour having an odd number of sides.

A word is any finite sequence of the letters A and B. There are two operations on words: 1) insert A anywhere in the word and append B at the end of the word; 2) insert AB anywhere in the word. Prove that the words that can be obtained from the word AB using only the first operation are exactly the words that can be obtained from the word AB using only the second operation.

In a tetrahedron $ABCD$ the edge $AB$ is perpendicular to $CD$, and $O$ is an arbitrary point in space. Prove that the sum of the squares of the distances from $O$ to the midpoints of the edges $AC$ and $BD$ equals the sum of the squares of the distances from $O$ to the midpoints of $AD$ and $BC$.

A tram ticket is called lucky in the Leningrad sense if the sum of its first three digits equals the sum of its last three digits. A tram ticket is called lucky in the Moscow sense if the sum of its digits in even positions equals the sum of its digits in odd positions. How many tickets are lucky both in the Leningrad and in the Moscow sense, including the ticket $000\,000$?

A group of $60$ holiday-makers arrives at a rest home with four meals a day for $15$ days. The dining table has $61$ seats. The director of the rest home always sits in one of them. The director wants to get acquainted with each holiday-maker himself and to get all of them acquainted with each other. For this purpose he wants to seat the holiday-makers differently each time, so that none of them sits twice in the same seat and so that every holiday-maker and the director has a new right-hand neighbour each time. How can this be done?

$K>1$ is a natural number. The sequence $(x_n)$ is defined as follows: $x_1=1$, $x_2=K$, $x_n=Kx_{n-1}-x_{n-2}$ for $n>2$. Prove that for every natural $n$ there exists $m>n$ such that $x_m-1$ and $x_n$ are coprime.
Construct a sequence of natural numbers such that among the differences between its terms every natural number occurs exactly once.

$AA'$, $BB'$ and $CC'$ are the altitudes of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ whose corresponding sides have lengths $a$, $b$ and $c$. $A_1$ and $A_2$ are the projections of $A'$ onto the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively, $B_1$ and $B_2$ are the projections of $B'$ onto the sides $BC$ and $BA$ respectively, and $C_1$ and $C_2$ are the projections of $C'$ onto the sides $CA$ and $CB$ respectively. Prove that $$a^2S(A'A_1A_2)+b^2S(B'B_1B_2)+c^2S(C'C_1C_2)=\frac{S^3}{R^2},$$ where $S$ is the area of the triangle $ABC$ and $R$ is the radius of its circumcircle.
What is the least number of discs of radius $1$ that can cover a disc of radius $1.5$?

Fifty gangsters have gathered in a square. They all shoot simultaneously, each at the gangster nearest to him or at one of the nearest ones (the gangsters never miss and kill outright). What is the least possible number of killed gangsters?
The sum of the positive numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ equals $1$. Prove that $$\sum_{i<j}\frac{a_ia_j}{a_i+a_j}\leqslant\frac{n-1}{4}.$$
The plane is coloured in three colours. Prove that one can find in it a triangle of area $1$ all of whose vertices have the same colour.

A square corner of side $0.001$ is cut out of a square of side $1\,000\,000$. The rest of the square is divided into $10$ rectangles. Prove that in at least one of them the ratio of the side lengths is greater than nine.
The centres of four equal circles are at the vertices of a square. Construct the quadrilateral of the largest perimeter with vertices on these circles.
$F_1, F_2, \ldots, F_n$ are polynomials with integer coefficients. Prove that for some integer $a$ all the numbers $F_1(a), F_2(a), \ldots, F_n(a)$ are composite.
$x_0<x_1<\ldots<x_n$ are natural numbers. Prove the inequality $$\frac{\sqrt{x_1-x_0}}{x_1}+\ldots+\frac{\sqrt{x_n-x_{n-1}}}{x_n}<1+\frac12+\frac13+\ldots+\frac{1}{n^2}.$$

A ball and a cube are inscribed in a triangular pyramid, all vertices of the cube lying on the faces of the pyramid. Prove that the ratio of the edge of the cube to the radius of the ball lies between the numbers $1$ and $1+\sqrt{2}$.
Prove the inequality $$\sin 2+\cos 2+2(\sin 1-\cos 1)\geqslant 1.$$
All angles of an equilateral pentagon are less than $120$ degrees. Prove that all of them are obtuse.
Positive numbers $a, b, c, d$ satisfy $a^2+b^2=c^2+d^2$ and $a^3+b^3=c^3+d^3$. Prove that $ab=cd$.
Find a function $f(x)$ such that $f(1/x)+f(1-x)=x$ for every real $x$ other than $0$ and $1$.

An $N\times N$ square is divided into three vertical strips. The width of the first strip from the left is $k$ cells and that of the third is $m$ cells, where the numbers $N-k$ and $N-m$ are coprime. The numbers from $1$ to $N$ are written in order from left to right in the first row. In the second row one writes from left to right first the numbers of the third strip of the first row without changing their order, then those of the second strip and finally those of the first strip, also without changing the order. The third row is obtained from the second row in the same way, and so on, until the whole square is filled. Prove that every column contains all the numbers from $1$ to $N$.

A natural number has the property that deleting any one of its digits yields a number divisible by $7$. Prove that either it is written only with fours or its decimal representation contains no four at all.

The numbers $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n$ are positive and their product equals $1$. Prove that there is an index $k\leqslant n$ such that $t_k(t_{k+1}+1)\geqslant 2$ (here $t_{n+1}$ denotes the number $t_1$).

A plane convex polygon is bent out of wire. Prove that it is impossible to bend out of this wire another (non-congruent) plane polygon in such a way that the distances between any two points of the wire do not increase.

Natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ satisfy $0<a_1<a_2<\ldots$ and $a_n<2n$ for every $n$. Prove that every natural number can be represented as the difference of two numbers of this sequence or is itself a number of the sequence.

$D$ and $C$ are arbitrary points of a circle that touches the segment $AB$ at its midpoint. $AD$ and $BC$ meet the circle again at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively, and $CX$ and $DY$ meet $AB$ at points $M$ and $N$ respectively. Prove that $AM=BN$.

The beginnings of the number $2345$ are the numbers $2, 23, 234, 2345$; its ends are the numbers $5, 45, 345, 2345$. These notions are defined similarly for all natural numbers. Natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$ having $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$ digits respectively are such that no beginning of any of these numbers is an end of another of these numbers; no beginning of a number other than the number itself is an end of that same number; and none of the numbers $a_i$ is a part of another number. Prove that $$\frac{n_1}{10^{n_1}}+\frac{n_2}{10^{n_2}}+\ldots+\frac{n_k}{10^{n_k}}<1,$$ given that $n_i<2n_j$ for all $i$ and $j$.

A real number is written in each cell of an infinite sheet of squared paper so that the sum of the numbers inside any square whose sides go along grid lines has absolute value at most $1$. Prove that the sum of the numbers inside any rectangle whose sides go along grid lines does not exceed $10000$.

Suppose that in the situation of the previous problem it is also known that in one of the rectangles the sum of the numbers has the maximal absolute value. Prove that in every rectangle the absolute value of the sum of the numbers does not exceed $4$.
A natural number $n$ is such that $n+1$ is divisible by $24$. Prove that the sum of all divisors of $n$, including $1$ and $n$ itself, is divisible by $24$.
In a tetrahedron one of the altitudes intersects two others. Prove that all the altitudes pass through one point.
Two flies crawl along two skew lines in space with equal constant speeds. Prove that there is a point in space that is always equidistant from both flies.
Prove that $$\left(\frac12\right)^{200}+\left(\frac12\right)^{199}\cdot\frac12+\left(\frac12\right)^{198}\cdot\frac13+\ldots+\frac12\cdot\frac{1}{200}+\frac{1}{201}<\frac{1}{90}.$$
Prove that if the numbers $2^1, 2^2, 2^4, 2^8, \ldots$ are written one after another after "zero point", the resulting number is irrational.

$N$ pairwise non-parallel lines and a point $P$ are given in the plane. The point $P$ is projected onto all the given lines, the projections obtained are again projected onto all the lines, and so on. Prove that all the points obtained in this way can be covered by one disc.
The real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are positive. Prove that the equation $$x^n+a_1x^{n-1}-a_2x^{n-2}-\ldots-a_n=0$$ has at most one positive root.

A collection of real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ is given. For $k\leqslant n$ denote by $A_k$ the largest of the numbers $$a_k,\ \frac{a_{k-1}+a_k}{2},\ \ldots,\ \frac{a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_k}{k}.$$ Prove that the smallest of the numbers $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ does not exceed the arithmetic mean of the numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$.

An arbitrary line is drawn through the vertex $A$ of a triangle $ABC$; $B_1$ and $C_1$ are the projections of the points $B$ and $C$ onto it; $B_2$ is the projection of $B_1$ onto $AC$; $C_2$ is the projection of $C_1$ onto $AB$. Prove that the intersection point of the lines $B_1B_2$ and $C_1C_2$ lies on one of the altitudes of the triangle $ABC$ or on its extension.

$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ are integers whose sum equals $1$. For $k\leqslant n$ denote by $N_k$ the number of positive numbers in the collection $$b_k,\ b_k+b_{k+1},\ b_k+b_{k+1}+b_{k+2},\ \ldots,\ b_k+b_{k+1}+\ldots+b_n+b_1+\ldots+b_{k-1}.$$ Prove that all the numbers $N_k$ are distinct.

A square of side $n-1$ and a rectangle with sides $a-1$ and $b-1$ are divided into unit squares; $ab=n^2$. To each of the $n^2$ nodes of the square one node of the rectangle is assigned, different nodes being assigned to different nodes. It is known that the four vertices and the centre of every $2\times 2$ square are assigned, respectively, the four vertices and the centre of a parallelogram whose vertices and centre are grid nodes of the rectangle (the parallelogram may be degenerate). Prove that $a=b$, given that $a,b>2$.

The edges of a complete graph with $2n+1$ vertices are coloured in three colours. Prove that one can choose one of the colours and $n+1$ vertices of the graph so that from each of the chosen vertices one can reach any other chosen vertex along edges of the chosen colour.
Prove that the equation $x^3+y^3+z^3=2$ has infinitely many integer solutions.

A chip of wood floated along both sections of a river having the shape shown in the figure. Prove that a raft can be nailed to the chip having such a shape that, when the chip repeats the same path, the raft floats along the river touching the banks with all points of its edge.

The numbers $a, b, c$ lie between $0$ and $1$. Prove that $$a+b+c-2\sqrt{abc}\geqslant ab+bc+ac-2abc.$$

A closed broken line in space is called regular if all its segments are equal and all angles between neighbouring segments are equal. Prove that for every $N$ greater than $5$ there exists a regular closed $N$-segment broken line not lying in one plane.
A prime $p$ is different from $3$. Prove that the number $4p^2+1$ can be represented as a sum of three squares of natural numbers.

$AC$ is the longest side of a triangle $ABC$. Segments $AC_1=AB$ and $CA_1=CB$ are laid off on it. Segments $AA_2=AA_1$ and $CC_2=CC_1$ are laid off on the sides $AB$ and $CB$. Prove that the points $A_1$, $A_2$, $C_1$ and $C_2$ lie on one circle.
An equilateral triangle of area $1$ lies inside a convex heptagon of area $1.0000001$. Prove that at least one of the angles of the heptagon is greater than $139^\circ$.

Several matches have been played in a volleyball tournament, after which every team has $10$ wins and $10$ losses. Prove that one can choose several of the matches played so that in them every team that took part in the tournament has exactly one loss and exactly one win.
Find the maximum of the ratio $k^2/(1.01)^k$ over natural $k$ and indicate all $k$ at which it is attained.
Prove that a line that bisects the area of a triangle divides its perimeter in a ratio of at most $3:1$.
Ninety-nine nines are written in a row. Prove that one can append $100$ digits to them on the right so that the resulting number is a perfect square.
A point $M$ is taken on the side $BC$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$. Prove that among the circles inscribed in the triangles $ABD$, $ACD$ and $AMD$ there are two with different radii.
In a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers, each number from the third on equals the sum of some two preceding ones. Prove that this sequence contains infinitely many composite numbers.

Each side of an equilateral triangle is divided into $30$ equal parts. The lines drawn through the division points parallel to the sides of the triangle divide it into $900$ small triangles. What is the largest number of vertices of the subdivision no two of which lie on a drawn line or on a side?

The city of Metropolis has $1972$ metro stations. Each metro line connects only two stations. It is known that after closing any $9$ stations the metro system remains connected. It is also known that from some station A to some station B at least $99$ changes are needed. Prove that all the metro stations can be divided into $1000$ groups so that no two stations in the same group are connected by a metro line.

A city has the form of a $100\times 100$ square grid with cells of side $500$ metres. Along each side of each cell one may move in only one direction. It is known that one can drive at most one kilometre through the city without breaking the traffic rules. Prove that there are at least $1300$ crossroads from which one cannot leave without breaking the traffic rules. (The corners of the city are also crossroads.)
$AD$ and $BE$ are angle bisectors of a triangle $ABC$. Prove that if $AC>BC$, then $AE>DE>BD$.
Prove that if an infinite geometric progression can be extracted from an infinite arithmetic progression with first term $A$ and non-zero common difference $d$, then $A/d$ is a rational number.

Prove that $$\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\cdot\left(1-\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\right)+2\cos\frac{\pi}{8}\cdot\left(1-\cos\frac{\pi}{8}\right)+\ldots+256\cos\frac{\pi}{1024}\cdot\left(1-\cos\frac{\pi}{1024}\right)<\frac12.$$
Prove that a convex polyhedron has two faces with the same number of sides.

A convex $1973$-gon, a point $O$ inside it and an acute angle $\alpha$ are given. It is known that however an angle equal to $\alpha$ with vertex $O$ is constructed, the area of the common part of the polygon and the angle is the same. Prove that the polygon is regular.

Ten white and twenty black counters are placed around a circle. It is allowed to swap any two counters between which there are exactly three other counters. Two arrangements of the counters (at the given $30$ points) are called equivalent if one of them can be transformed into the other by several such swaps. How many non-equivalent arrangements are there?
It is known that the sum of the absolute values of the pairwise differences of five non-negative numbers equals $1$. Find the smallest possible value of the sum of these numbers.

$2k+3$ points in general position are given in the plane, no four of them lying on one circle. Prove that a circle can be drawn through three of them containing exactly $k$ of the given points inside.

A polynomial $P(x)=a_0x^n+\ldots+a_{n-1}x+a_n$ with all coefficients integers is given. It is known that the equations $P(x)=1$, $P(x)=2$, $P(x)=3$ have integer roots. Prove that the equation $P(x)=5$ cannot have two or more integer roots.

Several volleyball teams played a single round-robin tournament. It is known that if A beat B, then there is a team C that lost to A but beat B. What is the least number of teams that could take part in the tournament?

A square of side $1$ is given. A quadrilateral is inscribed in it, and a square with sides parallel to the sides of the large square is inscribed in this quadrilateral. Prove that if the sides of the small square have length $1/2$, then the vertices of this square bisect the sides of the inscribed quadrilateral.

A convex polygon of area $9$ is given. It is intersected by nine parallel lines at unit distances from one another. Prove that the sum of the lengths of the segments cut out by the polygon on these lines is at most $10$.

Two people play. One thinks of a ten-digit number, and the other may ask him which digits stand at a specified set of positions in its decimal representation. The first answers him, but without indicating which digits stand at which positions. What is the least number of questions that certainly suffices to guess the number?
A cube of edge $A$ is thrown onto squared paper. Prove that it cannot cover more than $(A+1)^2$ lattice points.
Is there a $20$-digit perfect square whose decimal representation begins with $11$ ones?

Rays $OS_1$, $OS_2$, $OS_3$ issuing from a point $O$ meet three parallel planes at the points $A_1, B_1, C_1$; $A_2, B_2, C_2$; $A_3, B_3, C_3$ respectively. Let $V$ be the volume of the pyramid $OA_1B_2C_3$. Denote the volumes of the pyramids $OA_1B_1C_1$, $OA_2B_2C_2$, $OA_3B_3C_3$ by $V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$ respectively. Prove that $V\leqslant (V_1+V_2+V_3)/3$.

Find the maximum of the expression $$x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4-x_1x_2-x_1x_3-x_1x_4-x_2x_3-x_2x_4-x_3x_4+x_1x_2x_3+x_1x_2x_4+x_1x_3x_4+x_2x_3x_4-x_1x_2x_3x_4$$ for $|x_1|\leqslant 1$, $|x_2|\leqslant 1$, $|x_3|\leqslant 1$, $|x_4|\leqslant 1$.
Prove that there is no finite set of $n$ points in space ($n>4$) such that for any three of its points there is a fourth point of the set forming a parallelogram with the first three.

A point $O$ is given in the plane, from which $12$ rays issue; neighbouring rays form angles less than $\pi/4$. A point $A_1$ is marked on the ray $S_1$ at distance $729$ from $O$. Through $A_1$ a line parallel to the ray $S_{12}$ is drawn until it meets the ray $S_2$ at a point $A_2$. Through $A_2$ a line parallel to the ray $S_1$ is drawn until it meets the ray $S_3$ at a point $A_3$, and so on. Finally the point $A_{13}$ on the ray $S_1$ is constructed. Prove that $|OA_{13}|\leqslant 1$.

The number $2^n$ is written on the board. Under it two natural numbers with sum equal to the original number are written. Then under each of the numbers obtained successively two natural numbers with sum equal to it are written, until a one appears. Prove that the sum of all numbers written is at least $n2^n$.
$37$ point satellites are flying above a spherical planet. Prove that at any moment there is a point on the surface of the planet from which at most $17$ satellites are visible.

In a certain group of people, every two people having the same number of acquaintances in the group have no common acquaintances. Prove that in this group either nobody knows anybody, or somebody has exactly one acquaintance.
Prove that a convex polygon with an even number of sides has a diagonal not parallel to any of the sides.

Natural numbers are written in the cells of a rectangular table. It is allowed to double simultaneously all numbers of one column or to subtract one from all numbers of a row. Prove that by such operations one can obtain a table consisting only of zeros.

The sides of a square are numbered consecutively $1, 2, 3, 4$. For an arbitrary point $A$ and a side $k$, denote by $A_k$ the point symmetric to the projection of $A$ onto the line $k$ with respect to the point $A$. Find all points $A$ such that each of the points $A_1, A_{12}, A_{123}, A_{1234}, A_{12341}, \ldots$ lies inside our square.
The sum of one hundred natural numbers less than $100$ equals $200$. Prove that one can choose several of them whose sum equals $100$.

Find all natural numbers $k$ with the property that there is no $k$-gon such that on the extension of each of its sides there lies another side of this $k$-gon. Only polygons with non-parallel neighbouring sides are considered.

A prime $p$ is given. Prove that from any $p+1$ pairwise distinct natural numbers one can choose two numbers such that the ratio of the larger of them to their greatest common divisor is at least $p+1$.
There are $1975$ geometric progressions all of whose terms are integers. Prove that they do not exhaust the natural numbers.
Among the triangles contained in a given triangle, find the triangle with the largest ratio of area to perimeter.
Solve the equation $x^2+2=4\sqrt{x^3+1}$.
Four balls of the same radius are given in space. Prove that no three of them cover the fourth ball.
Some cells of a $100\times 100$ square table are coloured. Each coloured cell is the only coloured cell either in its column or in its row. What is the largest number of cells that can be coloured?
A convex $N$-gon is contained in a $1\times 1$ square. Prove that there are three consecutive vertices of this $N$-gon such that the area of the triangle formed by them is at most $8/N^2$.
The numbers $a, b, c, d$ satisfy $a^2+b^2=c^2+d^2=1$ and $ac+bd=0$. Find the number $ab+cd$.
Do there exist in space four pairwise disjoint balls not containing a given point $A$ such that every ray starting at $A$ meets at least one of these balls?

In a country some cities are connected by roads. The length of each road is at most $500$ kilometres. It is known that one can get from any city to any other city travelling at most $500$ kilometres. One of the roads was closed, and it is still possible to get from every city to every other. Prove that now this can be done travelling at most $1500$ kilometres.
Does there exist a bijection $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x)+f^{-1}(x)=-x$ for every $x$?
The centres of all $64$ cells of a chessboard are marked. Can the board be divided into parts by thirteen straight cuts so that each part contains at most one centre of a cell?
A sequence of integers $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots$ satisfies $x_0=0$ and $|x_n|=|x_{n-1}+1|$ for every natural $n$. What is the smallest possible value of the expression $|x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_{1975}|$?

Points $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$ on the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$ of a triangle $ABC$ are chosen so that the segments $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ meet at a point $D$. The segments $A_1C_1$ and $BB_1$ meet at a point $E$. Prove that if $BD=2B_1D$, then $BE=B_1E$.

Each of the numbers $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n$ equals $0$ or $1$. Prove that $$x_0+\frac{x_1}{\sqrt2}+\frac{x_2}{(\sqrt2)^2}+\ldots+\frac{x_n}{(\sqrt2)^n}\leqslant(1+\sqrt2)\sqrt{x_0+\frac{x_1}{2}+\ldots+\frac{x_n}{2^n}}.$$

A closed four-segment broken line all of whose segments have equal length is given in space. Prove that the distance from any point of space to any vertex of the broken line is less than the sum of the distances from this point to the three other vertices.
Find the function $f$ defined on the set of all real numbers if it is known that $f^2(x+y)=f^2(x)+f^2(y)$ for all $x$ and $y$.
Find all real solutions of the equation $$\sqrt{a+bx}+\sqrt{b+cx}+\sqrt{c+ax}=\sqrt{b-ax}+\sqrt{c-bx}+\sqrt{a-cx},$$ given that it has solutions.
The sides of a triangle have lengths $a, b, c$. Prove that $$2<\frac{a+b}{c}+\frac{b+c}{a}+\frac{c+a}{b}-\frac{a^3+b^3+c^3}{abc}\leqslant 3.$$

A $5\times 5$ table is filled with zeros and ones. It is known that there are ones in the upper left and lower right corners and zeros in the two other corners. Prove that one can choose in the table two different $2\times 2$ squares (possibly overlapping) with the same arrangement of numbers.

$K$ is the intersection point of the bisectors of the interior angle $B$ and the exterior angle $C$ of a triangle $ABC$, and $L$ is the intersection point of the bisectors of the interior angle $C$ and the exterior angle $B$. Prove that the midpoint of the segment $KL$ lies on the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.
In a convex pentagon $ABCDE$ all sides are equal, and the angle $ACE$ equals half the angle $BCD$. Find the angle $ACE$.
Space is partitioned into five non-empty subsets. Prove that there is a line meeting at least three of them.
Solve the system in real numbers: $$\begin{cases} x_1+x_2=x_3^2\\ x_2+x_3=x_4^2\\ x_3+x_4=x_5^2\\ x_4+x_5=x_1^2\\ x_5+x_1=x_2^2. \end{cases}$$

Two players play a game with a finite number of positions, and for every position the sum of the number of positions to which one can move from it and the number of positions from which one can move to it is one and the same. A player who has no move loses. Prove that the number of positions in which the player to move loses under correct play of the second player is at most half the number of all positions.

All cells of a $100\times 100$ table are painted in three colours. It is allowed to repaint any $2\times 2$ square in the colour that predominates in it, and if there is no such colour, in the colour that is absent from the square. Prove that the whole square can be repainted in one colour.

The plane is divided into equal equilateral triangles. One hundred triangles are painted black so that they form a connected figure. Prove that one can cut out of this figure at least $33$ non-overlapping rhombi, each consisting of two triangles.
Prove that among the $1976$-digit numbers whose decimal representation consists of $1975$ ones and one seven, at least $658$ are composite.

$F$ is a bijection of the plane onto itself such that whenever $ABCD$ is a convex non-degenerate quadrilateral, the quadrilateral $F(A)F(B)F(C)F(D)$ is also non-degenerate and convex. Prove that if the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on one line, then the points $F(A)$, $F(B)$, $F(C)$ also lie on one line.
Prove that if $0<x<\pi/2$, then $\sin x\cdot\tan x>x^2$.
How many vertices can a convex polyhedron have if all coordinates of each vertex are integers, while every other point inside it or on its boundary has at least one non-integer coordinate?
$P$ is a natural number greater than $1$; $n$ and $k$ are natural numbers. Prove that at least one of the numbers $\binom{n}{k}, \binom{n+1}{k}, \ldots, \binom{n+k}{k}$ is not divisible by $P$.
Prove that the sum of all dihedral angles of a triangular pyramid is greater than $360$ degrees.

Real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{1977}$ satisfy $a_1\geqslant a_2\geqslant\ldots\geqslant a_{1977}$. Prove that $$a_1^2-a_2^2+\ldots+(-1)^{1976}a_{1977}^2\geqslant\left(a_1-a_2+a_3-\ldots+(-1)^{1976}a_{1977}\right)^2.$$

The function $f$ is defined on $[0;1)$ by the rule $$f(x)=\begin{cases} x+\dfrac{2-\sqrt2}{2}, & \text{if } x\in\left[0;\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right),\\[2mm] x-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}, & \text{if } x\in\left[\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2};1\right). \end{cases}$$ Prove that for every interval $(a;b)\subset[0;1)$ there exist a point $x$ of this interval and a natural number $n$ such that the point $f(f(\ldots f(x)\ldots))$ ($n$ times) lies in the interval $(a;b)$.
A polynomial with positive leading coefficient takes prime values only at prime natural values of the argument. Prove that at all prime values of the argument the values of the polynomial are prime.
What is the largest possible number of equilateral triangles that can be formed in the plane by six intersecting lines?
A five-digit number is divisible by $41$. Prove that every five-digit number obtained from it by a cyclic permutation of its digits is also divisible by $41$.

Positive numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3, b_1, b_2, b_3$ satisfy the inequalities $$\sum_{i\leqslant j}a_ia_j\leqslant 1,\qquad\sum_{i\leqslant j}b_ib_j\leqslant 1.$$ Prove that $$\sum_{i\leqslant j}(a_i-b_i)(a_j-b_j)\leqslant 1.$$
A convex hexagon is given in which each main diagonal bisects its area. Prove that these diagonals meet at one point.
The cells of a $100\times 100$ board are coloured in four colours so that cells of the same colour have no common vertices. Prove that the corner cells of the board are coloured in different colours.

Let $A$ and $B$ be two finite sets in the plane. Put $d_H(A,B)=\max(d_1;d_2)$, where $d_1$ is the largest of the distances from the points of $A$ to the set $B$, and $d_2$ is the largest of the distances from the points of $B$ to the set $A$. Prove the triangle inequality for $d_H$, i.e. prove that for any three finite sets $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ in the plane $d_H(X,Y)+d_H(Y,Z)\geqslant d_H(X,Z)$.

Integers are placed at the vertices of a regular $100$-gon. Every minute each number is replaced by its difference with the number following it clockwise. Prove that after five minutes the sum of the numbers at the vertices of our $100$-gon is divisible by $5$.

$1978$ segments are given on a line, no two of which have a common endpoint. Prove that these segments cannot be numbered so that for every $k$ from $1$ to $1978$ the $k$-th segment contains exactly $k$ endpoints of the other segments.
A sequence $(a_n)$ all of whose terms equal $0$ or $1$ is such that if $k<2^n$, then $a_k\ne a_{k+2^n}$. Prove that it is not periodic.
$M$ is a convex polygon and $H$ is a homothety with ratio $-1/2$. Prove that there is a translation $T$ such that the polygon $T(H(M))$ lies inside the polygon $M$.

The vertices of a finite graph are coloured in two colours. Every second each vertex changes its colour to the colour of the majority of its neighbours. Prove that for each vertex there is a moment after which it either does not change its colour or changes it every second.

A convex polygon $M$ is given such that the lengths of all its sides and diagonals are integers. $K$ is a given square. Prove that there is a finite collection of polygons congruent to $M$ whose union contains $K$ and such that every point of the square not lying on a side of one of the polygons is covered by the same number of polygons of the collection.
Prove that if a $k$-digit number ($k\geqslant 2$) is prime, then either all numbers obtained from it by cyclic permutations of its digits are distinct, or the number is written only with ones.

A square hole $1\times 1$ is made in the centre of the bottom of a box having the shape of a $5\times 5$ square. What is the smallest area that a convex figure (a "shutter") must have in order to cover the hole in any position on the bottom of the box?
For which natural $y$ is the number $y^2+3^y$ a perfect square?

$n$ sectors of a disc are painted so that the angular size of each is less than $\pi/(n^2-n+1)$. Prove that the disc can be rotated so that all painted sectors move into the unpainted part of the disc.
A convex polyhedron is given. Prove that if all its faces except one are centrally symmetric polygons, then this last face is also centrally symmetric.

Two diameters $AB$ and $CD$ are drawn in a circle. Prove that for any two points $E$ and $F$ on the circle, the intersection point of the lines $AE$ and $DF$, the centre of the circle and the intersection point of the lines $CE$ and $BF$ lie on one line.

Three people play table tennis, and the player who loses a game gives up his place to the player who did not take part in it. In the end it turned out that the first player won $10$ games, the second $12$ and the third $14$. How many games did each player play?
How many different numbers occur in the sequence $$\left[\frac{1^2}{1980}\right],\ \left[\frac{2^2}{1980}\right],\ \ldots,\ \left[\frac{1980^2}{1980}\right]?$$
Do there exist numbers $a$ and $b$ such that for all $x$ in the segment $[0;2\pi]$ the inequality $$f^2(x)-f(x)\cos x<\frac14\sin x$$ holds, where $f(x)=ax+b$?

A midline of a convex quadrilateral is a segment joining the midpoints of opposite sides. Prove that if the sum of the lengths of the midlines of a quadrilateral equals its semiperimeter, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

Real numbers are written in the cells of an $N\times N$ square table. It is allowed to replace any two numbers by their arithmetic mean, written in both cells. Find all natural numbers $N$ for which, for every initial arrangement of numbers in the table, one can achieve by such operations that all cells contain equal numbers.
Prove that any two points on the surface of a regular tetrahedron with edge $1$ can be joined by a broken line running along the surface of the tetrahedron whose length does not exceed $2/\sqrt3$.

Two cockroaches sit on the boundary of a convex polygon. They simultaneously start moving along the boundary in the same direction with the same speed. For which initial positions of the cockroaches will the minimal distance between them during the motion be the largest?

In each of two congruent regular $16$-gons, $7$ vertices are marked. Prove that the polygons can be superposed so that at least four marked vertices of one polygon coincide with marked vertices of the other.

A triangle $ABC$ with vertices at lattice points is drawn on an infinite sheet of squared paper with cells of side $1$. Prove that if $AB>AC$, then $AB-AC>1/p$, where $p$ is the perimeter of the triangle $ABC$.
Integers $a, b, c, d$ and $A$ satisfy $a^2+A=b^2$, $c^2+A=d^2$. Prove that the number $2(a+b)(c+d)(ac+bd-A)$ is the square of a natural number.

Points $A_0$, $B_0$ and $C_0$ are marked on the lateral edges $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ of a triangular prism $ABCA_1B_1C_1$ so that $AA_0=a$, $BB_0=b$, $CC_0=c$. Let $M$ be the intersection point of the planes $A_0BC$, $B_0AC$, $C_0AB$, and let $MP$ be a segment drawn from it parallel to the lateral edges of the prism, with the point $P$ in the base $ABC$ and $MP=d$. Prove that $1/d=1/a+1/b+1/c$.

The squares of a $10\times 10$ board are coloured in two colours in a chessboard pattern. A counter moves on the black squares, and in one move it can go to any diagonally adjacent square. What is the smallest number of moves needed to visit all the black squares?
Is there a natural power of the number $5$ in whose last hundred decimal digits at least $30$ consecutive zeros occur?
Find all natural $p$ for which the number $$2^{2^{\cdot^{\cdot^{2}}}}+9$$ (with $p$ twos in the tower) is prime.

Points $C_1$, $B_1$ and $A_1$ are chosen on the sides $AB$, $AC$ and $BC$ respectively of an equilateral triangle $ABC$ of side $2$. What is the largest possible value of the sum of the radii of the circles inscribed in the triangles $AB_1C_1$, $A_1BC_1$ and $A_1B_1C$?

There is a pile of $m$ stones. Two players take turns removing stones from it, and on the $k$-th move one may take from $1$ to $k$ stones. The player who takes the last stone wins. For which $m$ does the first player have a winning strategy?
Prove that there are no rational numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ such that $(a+b\sqrt3)^4+(c+d\sqrt3)^4=1+\sqrt3$.

$16$ cells of a white $8\times 8$ square are painted black, with exactly two black cells in every column and in every row. Prove that the number of black cells cannot be decreased by recolouring rows and columns.

Do there exist six six-digit numbers, each consisting of the digits from $1$ to $6$ without repetitions, such that every three-digit number written only with digits from $1$ to $6$ without repetitions can be obtained from one of these numbers by deleting three digits?

$p$ numbers, each equal to $+1$ or $-1$, are written in a row. In one operation one may change the sign of several consecutive numbers simultaneously. What is the least number of such operations by which any such collection can be turned into a collection of ones only?
Do there exist in space five points with pairwise distinct mutual distances such that the perimeter of every spatial pentagon with vertices at these five points is the same?
The numbers $a, b, c$ lie in the segment $[0;1]$. Prove the inequality $$\sqrt{a(1-b)(1-c)}+\sqrt{b(1-a)(1-c)}+\sqrt{c(1-a)(1-b)}\leqslant 1+\sqrt{abc}.$$

Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_7$; $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_7$; $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_7$ be three collections of integers. Prove that one can delete several triples of numbers with equal indices (but not all of them!) so that in each collection the sum of the remaining numbers is divisible by $3$.

A sequence of digits is written whose first four terms are $1, 9, 8, 2$, and each subsequent digit is the last digit of the sum of the four preceding ones. Will the four consecutive digits $3, 0, 4, 4$ occur in this sequence?
The cells of a $5\times 41$ rectangle are coloured in two colours. Prove that one can choose three rows and three columns so that all nine cells at their intersections have the same colour.
It is given that $$\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}+\frac{a^2+c^2-b^2}{2ac}+\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}=1.$$ Prove that two of these three fractions equal $1$ and one equals $-1$.
In a tetrahedron $ABCD$ the sum of the angles $BAC$ and $BAD$ equals $180$ degrees. $AK$ is the bisector of the angle $CAD$. Find the angle $BAK$.

Prove that non-zero numbers can be placed at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon so that for every set of vertices of the original polygon forming a regular $k$-gon ($k\leqslant n$) the sum of the numbers placed at them equals zero.

$4n$ points are marked on a circle and coloured alternately red and blue. The points of each colour are split into pairs, and the points of each pair are joined by a segment of the same colour as the points (no three segments pass through one point). Prove that there are at least $n$ intersection points of red segments with blue ones.
Is there a natural number $k$ such that from any $180$ vertices of a regular $360$-gon with centre $O$ one can choose two vertices $A$ and $B$ with angle $AOB$ equal to $k$ degrees?

A square is divided into $9801=99^2$ equal small squares, and their centres are marked in all small squares except one corner square. The marked points are split into pairs, and the points of each pair are joined by a vector. Prove that the sum of the vectors obtained is not the zero vector.
$10$ points are taken on a circle. What is the largest number of segments with endpoints at these points that can be drawn so that no three of them form a triangle with vertices at the marked points?

Petya bought $8$ pies with rice and with cabbage and paid one rouble for them. Vasya bought $9$ pies and paid one rouble and one kopeck. How much does a pie with rice cost, if it is known that it is more expensive than a pie with cabbage and that the pies cost more than one kopeck?

$D$ and $E$ are the points of tangency of the incircle of a triangle $ABC$ with the sides $BC$ and $AC$. A perpendicular $BK$ is dropped to the bisector of the angle $BAC$. Prove that the points $D$, $E$ and $K$ lie on one line.

$(A_n)$ is an infinite sequence of natural numbers such that $A_{n+k}-A_k$ is divisible by $A_n$ for all $n$ and $k$. Denote by $B_n$ the product $A_1A_2\ldots A_n$. Prove that $B_{n+k}$ is divisible by $B_nB_k$ for all $n$ and $k$.

$N$ points are given in the plane, no three on one line and no four on one circle. Prove that there are at most $N-2$ circles each of which passes through three of the given points and contains all the other points inside it.

Prove that the set of all natural numbers greater than one cannot be partitioned into two non-empty sets so that whenever numbers $a$ and $b$ lie in the same set, the number $ab-1$ also lies in that set.

Two sequences of numbers $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are defined by $x_1=x_2=10$, $y_1=y_2=-10$ and $$x_{n+2}=(x_n+1)x_{n+1}+1,\qquad y_{n+2}=(y_{n+1}+1)y_n+1$$ for all natural $n$. Prove that every natural number occurs in at most one of these sequences.

Several children stand in a circle, each having some sweets. At the leader's signal each passes half of his sweets to the child standing on his right (if someone has an odd number of sweets, the leader first gives him one more sweet). This is repeated many times. Prove that at some moment all the children will have equal numbers of sweets.
For which $n\geqslant 2$ does the inequality $$x_1^2+x_2^2+\ldots+x_n^2\geqslant x_n(x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_{n-1})$$ hold for all real values of the variables $x_i$?

A trihedral angle is given. It is known that the bisectors of two of its plane angles are perpendicular. Prove that the plane through these bisectors is perpendicular to the plane of the third plane angle.
In a regular $20$-gonal pyramid the centre of the inscribed ball coincides with the centre of the circumscribed ball. Find the plane angles of a lateral face (in degrees).

Several points are placed on a circle. They start to move with constant speeds of equal magnitude (some clockwise and some counterclockwise). When two points collide, they fly apart, keeping the same magnitude of speed and remaining on the circle. Prove that there will be a moment when every point is in its initial position.
Nine vertices of a regular $20$-gon are marked. Prove that there is an isosceles triangle with vertices at marked points.

Prove that for every point of the plane, the area of the polygon obtained as the intersection of a given triangle $ABC$ with the triangle symmetric to it with respect to this point does not exceed $2/3$ of the area of the triangle $ABC$.

Two players take turns putting crosses and noughts in the cells of an infinite sheet of squared paper. The first wants some four crosses to form a square with sides parallel to the grid lines, and the second tries to prevent him. Can the first player win?
The angle $A$ at the apex of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ equals $100^\circ$. On the ray $AB$ a segment $AM$ equal to the base $BC$ is laid off. Find the angle $BCM$.
For which $n$ can $n$ numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ (not all zero) be placed around a circle so that for every $k\leqslant n$ the sum of $k$ consecutive numbers starting with $a_k$ equals zero?

An infinite sheet of squared paper is covered by a layer of $1\times 2$ rectangular tiles with sides along the grid lines. Prove that it can be covered by three more layers of tiles in the same way so that no tile lies exactly above another one.

An increasing sequence of natural numbers $(a_n)$ is such that every natural number that is not a term of the sequence can be represented in the form $a_k+2k$ for some natural $k$. Prove that $a_k<\sqrt2\,k$ for all $k$.

In the Land of Fools there are $n^2$ towns arranged in a square, the distance between neighbouring towns being $10$ kilometres. The towns are connected by a system of roads consisting of straight sections parallel to the sides of the square. What is the minimal length of such a road system if it is known that one can get from any town to any other?
Prove that the sum of the distances from an arbitrary point of space to three vertices of an isosceles trapezoid is greater than the distance from this point to the fourth vertex.
A set $A$ consists of natural numbers, and among any $100$ consecutive natural numbers there is a number from $A$. Prove that $A$ contains four distinct numbers $a, b, c, d$ such that $a+b=c+d$.
Prove that the difference of the squares of the lengths of two adjacent sides of a parallelogram is less than the product of the lengths of its diagonals.

After several operations of differentiation and of multiplication by $x+1$, performed in some order, the polynomial $x^8+x^7$ turned into $ax+b$. Prove that the difference of the integers $a$ and $b$ is divisible by $49$.
What is the largest value that the sum $$|x_1-1|+|x_2-2|+\ldots+|x_{63}-63|$$ can take if $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{63}$ are the numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 63$ in some order?
The numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 100$ are placed at the vertices of a $50$-gonal prism. Prove that the prism has an edge such that the numbers at its endpoints differ by at most $48$.

One and nine zeros are given. It is allowed to choose two numbers and replace each of them by their arithmetic mean. What is the smallest number that can end up in the place of the one after a series of such operations?
Prove that if the sum of the plane angles at the apex of a pyramid is greater than $180$ degrees, then each lateral edge of the pyramid is less than the semiperimeter of its base.
An integer $a$ is such that the number $3a$ can be represented in the form $x^2+2y^2$, where $x$ and $y$ are integers. Prove that the number $a$ can also be represented in this form.

Four points with integer coordinates are given in the coordinate plane. It is allowed to replace any of these points by the point symmetric to it with respect to any other of these points. Is it possible by several such operations to pass from the points $(0;0)$, $(0;1)$, $(1;0)$, $(1;1)$ to the points $(0;0)$, $(1;1)$, $(3;0)$, $(2;-1)$?

Two diametrically opposite points $A$ and $B$ (different from the points of tangency) are chosen on a circle tangent to the sides of an angle with vertex $O$. The tangent to the circle at $B$ meets the sides of the angle at points $C$ and $D$, and the line $OA$ at a point $E$. Prove that $BC=DE$.
Prove that there is a set $A$ of natural numbers such that every natural number not belonging to it is the arithmetic mean of two distinct numbers of $A$, while no number of $A$ has this property.

Integers $a, b, c, d, e$ are such that the numbers $a+b+c+d+e$ and $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2+e^2$ are divisible by an odd number $n$. Prove that the number $a^5+b^5+c^5+d^5+e^5-5abcde$ is also divisible by $n$.

In the sequence $1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, \ldots$ each term from the seventh on equals the last digit of the sum of the six preceding terms. Prove that the six consecutive numbers $0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1$ do not occur in this sequence.
Real numbers $a, b, c, x, y, z$ satisfy $a^x=bc$, $b^y=ca$, $c^z=ab$, where the numbers $a, b, c$ are positive and at least one of them is different from $1$. Prove that $x+y+z-xyz$ is an integer.

A circle with centre $O$ touches the sides of an angle at points $A$ and $B$. Through an arbitrary point $M$ of the segment $AB$ other than $A$ and $B$, a line perpendicular to the line $OM$ is drawn, meeting the sides of the angle at points $C$ and $D$. Prove that $MC=MD$.

The lines drawn perpendicular to the faces of a tetrahedron through the centres of the circles inscribed in these faces meet at one point. Prove that the sums of the lengths of opposite edges of this tetrahedron are equal.
Prove the inequality $$9<\int_0^3\sqrt[4]{x^4+1}\,dx+\int_1^3\sqrt[4]{x^4-1}\,dx<9.0001.$$
The sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ is defined by $x_1=0.001$, $x_{n+1}=x_n-x_n^2$. Prove that $x_{1001}<0.0005$.

A game for two players consists of a rectangular board $1\times 25$ divided into $25$ square cells, and $25$ counters. The cells are numbered consecutively $1, 2, \ldots, 25$. In one move a player either puts a new counter on one of the free cells or moves a counter already on the board to the nearest free cell with a larger number. Initially all cells are free. The game ends when all cells are occupied by counters, and the player who made the last move wins. The players move alternately. Who wins with correct play: the first player or his opponent?

The perimeter of a triangle is $100$ cm and its area is $100\ \text{cm}^2$. Three lines drawn parallel to the sides of the triangle at distance $1$ cm from them divide the triangle into seven parts, three of which are parallelograms. Prove that the sum of the areas of the parallelograms is less than $25\ \text{cm}^2$.

Each cell of a $100\times 100$ board is coloured in one of four colours so that every $2\times 2$ square contains all four colours. Prove that the corner cells of the board have different colours.

$20$ volleyball teams played a single round-robin tournament. Let $T$ be the number of triples of teams that have one win each in the matches among themselves. Prove that a) if each team won at least $9$ and at most $10$ matches, then $T=330$; b) $T\leqslant 330$.
A trapezoid with bases $a$ and $b$ is circumscribed about a circle of radius $R$. Prove that $ab\geqslant 4R^2$.
A sequence of natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ satisfies $a_1=1$ and $a_{k+1}-a_k$ equals $0$ or $1$ for all $k$. Prove that if $a_m=m/1000$ for some $m$, then there is $n$ such that $a_n=n/500$.

In the sequence $f_1, f_2, \ldots$ the first two terms equal $1$ and each of the others equals the sum of the two preceding ones. Prove that $$\frac{1}{f_1f_3}+\frac{1}{f_2f_4}+\frac{1}{f_3f_5}+\ldots+\frac{1}{f_{98}f_{100}}<1.$$
A sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ of natural numbers satisfies $a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}a_n+1$ for all $n$. Prove that for every $n>10$ the number $a_n-22$ is composite.

A class has equally many boys and girls. Each boy is friends with an even number of girls. Prove that one can choose a group of several boys so that every girl is friends with an even number of boys of this group.
Find all three-digit numbers that are $11$ times the sum of their digits.

In a square $ABCD$, a point $E$ is taken on the side $BC$, points $K$ and $M$ on the side $CD$, and a point $H$ on the side $AD$, so that $CE=CK$ and $DM=DH$. Prove that a circle can be circumscribed about the quadrilateral formed by the intersection of the angles $HBM$ and $EAK$.
What is the least value that the product of two positive numbers $a$ and $b$ can take if it is known that $ab=a+b$?
Find all positive solutions of the equation $$x^{1986}+1986^{1985}=x^{1985}+1986^{1986}.$$
Find some integers $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $$\frac{A}{999}+\frac{B}{1000}+\frac{C}{1001}=\frac{1}{999\cdot 1000\cdot 1001}.$$
Find the angle between the edge $AB$ and the face $ACD$ of the trihedral angle $ABCD$ with vertex $A$ if the angle $BAC$ equals $45^\circ$, $CAD$ equals $90^\circ$ and $BAD$ equals $60^\circ$.

The diameter of a set in the plane is the largest of the distances between two of its points (if it exists). It is known that the sum of the diameters of polygons $M_1, M_2, \ldots, M_n$ is less than the diameter of their union. Prove that there is a line meeting none of the polygons such that on each side of it there lies at least one of them.
A function $F\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous. For every real $x$ there is a natural $n$ such that $F(F(\ldots F(x))\ldots)=1$ (the symbol $F$ written $n$ times). Prove that $F(1)=1$.
Prove that $$\frac{1}{1+\sqrt3}+\frac{1}{\sqrt5+\sqrt7}+\ldots+\frac{1}{\sqrt{9997}+\sqrt{9999}}>24.$$

In a parallelogram $ABCD$ that is not a rhombus, the bisector of the angle $BAD$ is drawn; $X$ and $Y$ are its intersection points with the lines $BC$ and $CD$ respectively. Prove that the centre of the circle through the points $C$, $X$ and $Y$ lies on the circle through the points $B$, $C$ and $D$.
Compute the integral $$\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{dx}{1+x^3+\sqrt{1+x^6}}.$$
Prove that one can place several discs in the plane, no two having common interior points, so that every disc touches exactly five others.

Given $$u_1=ax+by+cz,\quad v_1=ax+bz+cy,$$ $$u_2=ay+bz+cx,\quad v_2=az+by+cx,$$ $$u_3=az+bx+cy,\quad v_3=ay+bx+cz,$$ where $a, b, c, x, y, z$ are real numbers. It is known that $u_1u_2u_3=v_1v_2v_3$. Prove that the triple $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ can be obtained by permuting the numbers in the triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$.

There is a sheet of squared paper of $30\times 30$ cells. Two players play the following game: in one move (they move in turn) a cut is made along a line joining two adjacent grid nodes. The first player starts cutting from the edge of the sheet, and each subsequent cut must continue the line formed by the previous cuts. The player after whose move the sheet falls into two pieces wins. Who wins with correct play?

There is an unlimited supply of coins of denominations $1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50$ kopecks and $1$ rouble. It is known that $a$ kopecks can be changed using $b$ coins. Prove that then $b$ roubles can be changed using $a$ coins.
Compute $$\cfrac{1}{2-\cfrac{1}{2-\cfrac{1}{\ddots\, 2-\cfrac{1}{2}}}}\qquad(100\text{ twos}).$$

At the intersection points $A$ and $B$ of two circles, the tangents to these circles are perpendicular. Let $M$ be an arbitrary point of one of the circles lying inside the other circle. Extend the segments $AM$ and $BM$ beyond $M$ until they meet the circle containing $M$ inside it at points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that $XY$ is a diameter of this circle.
Arbitrary real numbers $a, b, c, d$ are given. Prove that $(1+ab)^2+(1+cd)^2+(ac)^2+(bd)^2\geqslant 1$.
Is there a natural number $n$ such that $n^n+(n+1)^n$ is divisible by $1987$?

An astronomer observing $50$ stars in the sky found that the sum of all pairwise distances between them equals $S$. A cloud covered $25$ of the stars. Prove that the sum of the pairwise distances between the visible stars is less than $S/2$.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the angle $B$ equals $60^\circ$, and the altitudes $CE$ and $AD$ meet at a point $O$. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $ABC$ lies on the common bisector of the angles $AOE$ and $COD$.
Continuous functions $f, g\colon[0;1]\to[0;1]$ have the property that $f(g(x))=g(f(x))$ for every $x$ in $[0;1]$. Prove that if $f$ is increasing, then there is $a\in[0;1]$ such that $f(a)=g(a)=a$.

Eight non-negative real numbers with sum equal to one are placed at the vertices of a cube. For each edge the numbers at its endpoints were multiplied. Prove that the sum of all products obtained in this way does not exceed $1/4$.

A sequence of real numbers $X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots$ and a natural number $T$ are given. Prove that if among all ordered $T$-tuples of the form $(X_{k+1}, X_{k+2}, \ldots, X_{k+T})$ there are at most $T$ different ones, then the sequence $X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots$ is periodic.

The diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at a point $O$. Prove that $$\frac{|AB|}{|CD|}+\frac{|CD|}{|AB|}+\frac{|BC|}{|AD|}+\frac{|AD|}{|BC|}\leqslant\frac{|OA|}{|OC|}+\frac{|OC|}{|OA|}+\frac{|OB|}{|OD|}+\frac{|OD|}{|OB|}.$$
Factor the number $989\cdot 1001\cdot 1007+320$ into primes.

A pile of $2n+1$ cards is given, with which the following two operations are allowed: a) some cards are taken from the top and moved to the bottom keeping their order; b) the top $n$ cards are inserted, keeping their order, into the $n$ gaps between the bottom $n+1$ cards. Prove that using these operations one cannot obtain more than $2n(2n+1)$ different arrangements of the cards from the initial one.

In an $m$-element set, $s$ subsets containing $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_s$ elements respectively are chosen. It is known that none of these subsets is contained in another. Prove that $$\frac{1}{\binom{m}{a_1}}+\frac{1}{\binom{m}{a_2}}+\ldots+\frac{1}{\binom{m}{a_s}}\leqslant 1,$$ where $\binom{m}{a_k}=m!/(a_k!(m-a_k)!)$.
$x_1, x_2\geqslant 0$ and $x_1+x_2=1/2$. Prove that $$\frac{1-x_1}{1+x_1}\cdot\frac{1-x_2}{1+x_2}\geqslant\frac13.$$

$BB_1$ and $CC_1$ are altitudes of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ with angle $A$ equal to $30$ degrees; $B_2$ and $C_2$ are the midpoints of the sides $AC$ and $AB$ respectively. Prove that the segments $B_1C_2$ and $B_2C_1$ are perpendicular.
$a$, $b$ and $c$ are natural numbers such that $a^3$ is divisible by $b$, $b^3$ is divisible by $c$, and $c^3$ is divisible by $a$. Prove that $(a+b+c)^{13}$ is divisible by $abc$.

Functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are defined on the whole real line and take real values. For all real $x$ and $y$ the equality $f(x+g(y))=2x+y+5$ holds. Find the function $g(x+f(y))$ (express it explicitly in terms of $x$ and $y$).
One hundred consecutive natural numbers are given. Can they be arranged around a circle so that the product of any two neighbouring numbers is a perfect square?

In a regular hexagonal pyramid the centre of the circumscribed sphere lies on the surface of the inscribed sphere. Find the ratio of the radius of the circumscribed sphere to the radius of the inscribed sphere.

A snail crawls in the plane, turning through $90$ degrees after each metre of its path. What is the largest distance from its starting point at which it could be after crawling $300$ metres and making $99$ left and $200$ right turns in all?
A function $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous. For every real $x$ the equality $f(x)\cdot f(f(x))=1$ holds. It is known that $f(1000)=999$. Find $f(500)$.
Find two coprime four-digit natural numbers $A$ and $B$ such that for all natural $m$ and $n$ the numbers $A^m$ and $B^n$ differ by at least $4000$.

$N$ towns are joined to each other by $2N-1$ one-way roads. One can get from any town to any other without breaking the rules. Prove that there is a road after whose closure this property is preserved.

Points $M$ and $N$ are taken on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The circles constructed on the segments $BN$ and $CM$ as diameters meet at points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that $P$, $Q$ and the orthocentre $H$ of the triangle $ABC$ lie on one line.
A polynomial $P(x)$ with real coefficients is given. Prove that if $P(x)-P'(x)-P''(x)+P'''(x)\geqslant 0$ for every real $x$, then $P(x)\geqslant 0$ for every real $x$.

A word is an arbitrary finite sequence of zeros and ones. The tripling of a word $A$ is its threefold repetition $AAA$. For example, if $A=101$, then its tripling is the word $101101101$. One of the following two operations may be applied to words: 1) insert at an arbitrary place (including the beginning or the end) the tripling of any word; 2) delete the tripling of any word. For instance, from the word $0001$ one can obtain the words $0111001$ and $1$. Can the word $01$ be obtained from the word $10$ by such operations?

A convex $n$-gon is given in the plane. Let $a_k$ be the length of its $k$-th side and $d_k$ the length of its projection onto the line containing this side ($k=1, 2, 3, \ldots, n$). Prove that $$2<\frac{a_1}{d_1}+\frac{a_2}{d_2}+\ldots+\frac{a_n}{d_n}\leqslant 4.$$
Prove that for no real $a$, $b$ and $c$ can the three numbers $(b-c)(bc-a^2)$, $(c-a)(ca-b^2)$, $(a-b)(ab-c^2)$ be positive simultaneously.

A point $X$ is chosen on the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$. Prove that if the incircles of the triangles $ABX$ and $BCX$ touch each other, then the point $X$ lies on the incircle of the triangle $ABC$.

Draw in the plane the set of points with coordinates $(x;y)$ for which there exist two non-negative numbers $a$ and $b$ such that the larger of the numbers $a^2$, $b$ equals $x$ and the smaller of the numbers $b^2$, $a$ equals $y$.
The base of a pyramid is an equilateral polygon. Prove that if all plane angles at the apex of the pyramid are equal, then among the triangular lateral faces of the pyramid there are two equal ones.

After a chess tournament of $k$ rounds it turned out that the numbers of points scored by the participants form a geometric progression with natural common ratio greater than $1$. How many participants could there have been a) for $k=1989$? b) for $k=1988$?

A point $M$ is taken inside a triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle BMC=90^\circ+\frac12\angle BAC$, and the line $AM$ passes through the circumcentre of the triangle $BMC$. Prove that $M$ is the incentre of the triangle $ABC$.

A finite collection of distinct natural numbers has the following property: all their prime divisors do not exceed a given number $n$. Prove that the sum of the reciprocals of these numbers does not exceed $n$.

A number triangle whose first row consists of $n$ ones and whose second row consists of $n-1$ arbitrary integers (see the example for $n=6$ in the figure) has the following property: for any four numbers forming a small rhombus, where $a$ and $c$ are the two neighbouring numbers of one row and $b$ and $d$ are the numbers directly above and below them, the equality $ac=bd+1$ holds. It is known that all numbers in the triangle are non-zero. Prove that then all of them are integers.
