What is the largest possible area of a quadrilateral with side lengths $1, 4, 7, 8$?
How many real solutions does the equation $$\sin(\sin(\sin(\sin(\sin(x)))))=x/3$$ have?

The microcalculator "FN-89" performs only two operations: $X\mapsto 2X-1$ and $X\mapsto 2X$. Some natural number is entered into the microcalculator. Prove that by pressing the keys one can obtain from it a number that is a perfect fifth power.

A sequence of real numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ is such that for all $m$ and $n$ the inequality $$|a_m+a_n-a_{m+n}|\leqslant\frac{1}{m+n}$$ holds. Prove that this sequence is an arithmetic progression.

Two players play the following game. There is a board on which the number $1000$ is written, and a pile of $1000$ matches. In one move each player (they move alternately) may either take from the pile or put into it at most $5$ matches (initially neither player has any matches), and then the number of matches in the pile after this move is written on the board. The player after whose move a number already present on the board appears loses. Who wins with correct play: the first player or his partner?
Prove that if the triangle in problem 3 of this paper consists of natural numbers, then the number of different numbers occurring in it is at least $n/4$.
Find all solutions of the system of equations $$\begin{cases} x^2+y^2=6z\\ y^2+z^2=6x\\ z^2+x^2=6y. \end{cases}$$
The incircle of a triangle $ABC$ divides its side $AB$ into segments $AD$ and $DB$ of lengths $5$ and $3$ respectively. The angle $A$ equals $60^\circ$. Find the length of the side $BC$.
Prove that every arithmetic progression whose terms are natural numbers contains two terms with the same digit sum.
Is there a triangle all of whose side lengths are integers and one of whose medians has length one?
Four distinct natural numbers are given. Prove that twice their product is greater than the sum of all pairwise products of these numbers.
Can the plane be covered without overlapping by squares with side lengths $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, \ldots$ if each square may be used a) at most $10$ times? b) at most once?

problems.paper_label: City round, grade 11 (variant for physics-and-mathematics schools)
problems.problem: Can one form a six-digit number divisible by $11$ from the digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$, using each of them once?

problems.paper_label: City round, grade 11 (variant for physics-and-mathematics schools)
problems.problem: In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ the angle $B$ is right, and the diagonal $AC$, which is the bisector of the angle $A$, has the same length as the side $AD$. The altitude $DH$ is drawn in the triangle $ADC$. Prove that the line $BH$ bisects the segment $CD$.

problems.paper_label: City round, grade 11 (variant for physics-and-mathematics schools)
problems.problem: A polynomial $F$ with integer coefficients is such that $F(2)$ is divisible by $5$ and $F(5)$ is divisible by $2$. Prove that $F(7)$ is divisible by $10$.

problems.paper_label: City round, grade 11 (variant for physics-and-mathematics schools)
problems.problem: A positive real number $x$ satisfies $$x^n=x^{n-1}+x^{n-2}+\ldots+x+1.$$ Prove that $2>x>2-\frac{1}{n}$.

problems.paper_label: City round, grade 11 (variant for physics-and-mathematics schools)
problems.problem: Prove that space can be partitioned into regular octahedra and tetrahedra with integer edge lengths so that no ten of these polyhedra have equal edge lengths.
Natural numbers $a$ and $n$ are greater than one. Prove that the number of natural numbers less than $a^n-1$ and coprime to it is divisible by $n$.

Several smaller segments covering a segment lie in it. Half of each of them, the left or the right one, was thrown away. Prove that the remaining halves cover at least one third of the length of the original segment.
Is there a hexagon in the plane (possibly non-convex) all of whose diagonals except one are of equal length?

The upper edge of a $100\times 100$ squared board was glued to the lower edge, and the right edge to the left edge, so that the board took the shape of a "doughnut". Can one place $50$ rooks, red, blue and green, in its cells so that each red rook attacks at least two blue rooks, each blue rook at least two green ones, and each green rook at least two red ones?
In a triangle $ABC$ with angle $A$ equal to $120^\circ$, the angle bisectors $AF$, $BG$ and $CH$ are drawn. Prove that the angle $GFH$ is right.

In the kingdom of Olympia there are $100$ towns, and every two of them are joined by exactly one one-way road. It turned out that one cannot get from every town to every other town obeying the traffic rules. Prove that the king can choose one of the towns and, by reversing the directions of all roads entering and leaving it, achieve that one can get from every town to every other obeying the traffic rules.
A continuous function $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfies $f(x+f(x))=f(x)$ for every real $x$. Prove that the function $f$ is constant.

Several numbers with positive sum are placed around a circle. It is allowed to replace a triple of consecutive numbers $x, y, z$ by the triple $x+y, -y, z+y$ (in exactly this order). Prove that from the given collection of numbers exactly one collection consisting only of non-negative numbers can be obtained by these operations.
Non-negative real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are given. Prove the inequality $$\max(a^2-b,\,b^2-c,\,c^2-d,\,d^2-a)\geqslant\max(a^2-a,\,b^2-b,\,c^2-c,\,d^2-d).$$
Can the numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 100$ be divided into three groups so that the sum of the numbers in the first group is divisible by $102$, in the second by $203$ and in the third by $304$?

A point $P$ lies outside a circle with centre $O$. Lines $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ pass through $P$; $\ell_1$ touches the circle at $A$, and $\ell_2$ meets the circle at $B$ and $C$. The tangents to the circle at $B$ and $C$ meet at a point $X$. Prove that $AX$ and $PO$ are perpendicular.

A sequence of natural numbers $a_n$ is constructed by the following rule. Each term with an even index $a_{2n}$ is obtained from $a_{2n-1}$ by adding to it one of the digits of $a_{2n-1}$, and each term with an odd index $a_{2n+1}$ is obtained from $a_{2n}$ by subtracting from it one of the digits of this number. Only non-zero digits may be added or subtracted at each step. Prove that all terms of this sequence do not exceed $4a_1+44$.
Do there exist four distinct numbers such that any two of them, $x$ and $y$, satisfy the relation $$x^{10}+x^9y+x^8y^2+\ldots+xy^9+y^{10}=1?$$

Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively so that $\angle AXY=2\angle ACB$ and $\angle CYX=2\angle BAC$. Prove the inequality $$\frac{S(AXYC)}{S(ABC)}\leqslant\frac{|AX|^2+|XY|^2+|YC|^2}{|AC|^2}.$$

On the planet Tranai there are $1991$ towns, every two of which are joined by a road. Every day the Ministry of Construction closes three roads for repair, after which the Ministry of Transport introduces one-way traffic on one of the roads that are not closed. The Ministry of Construction does not close roads on which one-way traffic has already been introduced. Prove that the Ministry of Transport can achieve that one can get from any town to any other moving only in the permitted directions.

A black counter stands in the upper right corner of an $8\times 8$ board. In one move one may put a white counter on any square of the board and recolour all counters standing on the squares adjacent to it (i.e. having a common vertex with this square). Can one achieve that the whole board is filled with white counters?

$AB$ is a chord dividing a circle into two segments. $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the arcs into which the points $A$ and $B$ divide the circle. Under a rotation about the point $A$ through some angle, the point $B$ goes to a point $B'$ and the point $M$ to a point $M'$. Prove that the segments joining the midpoint of the segment $BB'$ with the points $M'$ and $N$ are perpendicular.
Real numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ lie in the segment $[-1;1]$, and the sum of their cubes equals zero. Prove that the sum $x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_n$ does not exceed $n/3$.

The following two operations may be applied to a natural number: a) multiplying it by any natural number; b) deleting zeros in its decimal representation. Prove that using these operations one can obtain a one-digit number from any number.

Two continuous functions $f, g\colon[0;1]\to[0;1]$ are given, and the function $f$ is monotonically increasing. Prove the inequality $$\int_0^1 f(g(x))\,dx\leqslant\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx+\int_0^1 g(x)\,dx.$$

A finite sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ is called $p$-balanced if all sums of the form $a_k+a_{k+p}+a_{k+2p}+\ldots$ ($k=1, 2, \ldots, p$) are equal. Prove that if a sequence with $50$ terms is $p$-balanced for $p=3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17$, then all its terms are zero.
Prove that the number $512^3+675^3+720^3$ is composite.

A template is an arbitrary set of $n$ vertices of a regular $2n$-gon. Is it true that there always exist $100$ rotations of the $2n$-gon such that the images of the template under these rotations cover the whole set of $2n$ vertices?
A unit square with marked vertices has one more point marked inside it. Prove that there are three marked points forming a triangle of area at most $1/8$.

Distinct quadratic trinomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ with leading coefficients equal to one are given. It is known that $f(1)+f(10)+f(100)=g(1)+g(10)+g(100)$. For which $x$ does the equality $f(x)=g(x)$ hold?

Some number of black and the same number of white checkers are placed around a circle. Let $A$ be the number of triples of consecutive checkers in which white predominates, and $B$ the number of triples of consecutive checkers in which black predominates. Prove that $A\leqslant 3B$.

In an acute-angled scalene triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$ are drawn. Points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are such that $D$, $E$ and $F$ are the midpoints of the segments $BX$, $CY$ and $AZ$ respectively. Prove that the circumcentres of the triangles $ACX$, $ABY$ and $BCZ$ are the vertices of a triangle congruent to the triangle $ABC$.
The sequence $(F_n)$ is defined as follows: $F_0=0$, $F_1=1$ and $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$ for every $n>1$. Prove that the terms of this sequence include no numbers of the form $7^k$.
Prove that for all positive $a$, $b$, $c$ the inequality $$-1\leqslant\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right)^{11}+\left(\frac{b-c}{b+c}\right)^{11}+\left(\frac{c-a}{c+a}\right)^{11}\leqslant 1$$ holds.

All cells of a $10\times 10$ table are coloured black and white, and there are cells of both colours. Prove that real numbers can be placed in the cells so that the number in any white cell is greater than the arithmetic mean of the numbers in the neighbouring cells, and the number in any black cell is less than the arithmetic mean of the numbers in the neighbouring cells (cells are neighbouring if they have a common side).
$n$ segments are given such that from any $n-1$ of them one can form an $(n-1)$-gon. Prove that from some three of them one can form a triangle.
Find all triples of natural numbers such that the product of any two numbers of the triple, increased by $1$, is divisible by twice the third number.
Prove that if a natural number $a$ is not a perfect square, then there is a natural number $n$ such that $a=[n+\sqrt n+1/2]$.

Natural numbers $n$ and $k$ with $n>k$ are given. Prove that every natural number less than $\binom{n}{k}$ can be represented in exactly one way as a sum $$\binom{a_1}{1}+\binom{a_2}{2}+\ldots+\binom{a_k}{k},$$ where $0\leqslant a_1<a_2<\ldots<a_k<n$; we set $\binom{n}{k}=0$ for $n<k$.

It is known that for any four lines in general position in the plane (i.e. no two parallel and no three through one point), the circumcircles of the four triangles formed by these lines pass through one point. Is there a collection of $45$ lines in general position for which all circumcircles of the triangles formed by them pass through one point?

A country has $100$ towns joined by roads so that even if any town $A$ closes all roads leaving it, one can still get from any town to any other (not counting, of course, the town $A$ itself). Prove that the country can be divided into two sovereign states with $50$ towns each so that in both states one can get from any town to any other.

Let $L(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k)$ be the number of ways to place in the cells of an $m\times n$ table $a_1$ ones, $a_2$ twos, $\ldots$, $a_k$ numbers $k$ so that in every row the numbers increase (not strictly) from left to right, and in every column the numbers increase strictly from top to bottom. Prove that the value of the function $L$ does not depend on the order of its arguments.
Several unit discs are placed in the plane. Is it true that one can always mark several points so that each disc contains exactly one marked point inside it?

Points $D$ and $E$ are marked on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively so that $BD+DE=BC$ and $BE+ED=AB$. It is also known that the quadrilateral $ADEC$ is cyclic. Prove that the triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.
Prove that no number of the form $3000\ldots001$ is a perfect square.
The function $f(x)=x^3-3x$ is defined on the whole real line. Prove that the function $f(f(f(f(f(f(f(x)))))))$ takes some value at least $1993$ times.

A point $M$ lies inside the diameter $AB$ of a circle $S$ and is not the centre of the circle. Arbitrary distinct points $P$ and $Q$ are taken on the circle on one side of the diameter $AB$ such that the segments $PM$ and $QM$ form equal angles with the diameter. Prove that all the lines $PQ$ pass through one point.

A country has $n$ towns, some of which are joined by roads, any two towns being joined by at most one road. The "degree" of a town is the number of roads leaving it. Let $2\leqslant k\leqslant n$ be a natural number. Prove that there are always $k$ towns whose degrees differ from each other by less than $k-1$.
Differentiable functions $f$ and $g$ defined on the segment $[0;1]$ are such that $f(0)=f(1)=1$ and the function $19f'g+93fg'$ is non-negative. Prove that $g(1)\geqslant g(0)$.

Let $n$ be an arbitrary natural number, and let all natural numbers from $n$ to $3n-1$ be written on the board. It is allowed to erase any two numbers $a$ and $b$ ($a\leqslant b$) and to write the number $a/2$ instead of them. Prove that when, after a series of such operations, one number remains on the board, it is less than one.
A sequence $(a_k)$ consists of positive numbers and satisfies $(a_{k+1}+k)a_k=1$ for every $k$. Prove that all its terms are irrational.
Prove that there exists a function $f(x)$ defined on $[0;+\infty)$ such that $f(f(\ldots(x)\ldots))=1+x+2\sqrt x$ (the function $f$ applied $45$ times).
Points $D$ and $F$ are marked on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively, and $E$ is the midpoint of the segment $DF$. Prove that $AD+FC\leqslant AE+EC$.

In a kingdom there are three kinds of roads joining towns: highway, country road and railway. From each town exactly one road of each of the three kinds leaves. It is known that one can get from any town to any other. Prove that one can visit all the towns without travelling along any road in both directions.
Prove that for all positive numbers $a_k$, $b_k$ ($k=1, 2, \ldots, n$) the inequality $$\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{a_kb_k}{a_k+b_k}\leqslant\frac{AB}{A+B}$$ holds, where $A=\sum a_k$ and $B=\sum b_k$.

A convex hexagon is such that on its three "even" sides one can construct inwards rectangles whose vertices coincide as shown in the figure. Prove that on the three other sides one can also construct a similar triple of rectangles.

A fly crawls along the boundary of each face of a convex polyhedron (so there are as many flies as faces), and all of them move clockwise around their faces. It is known that their speeds are at every moment at least $1$ mm/h. Prove that sooner or later some two flies will collide.

Two squares $A$ and $B$ separated by an odd number of squares are marked on the edge of a $1993\times 1993$ board. Prove that the number of ways to cover with $1\times 2$ dominoes the whole board without the square $A$ equals the number of ways to cover with dominoes the board without the square $B$.
A point $D$ is chosen on the side $AC$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$, and a point $E$ on the side $AB$, so that $AE=CD$. $M$ is the midpoint of the segment $DE$. Prove that $AM=\frac12 BD$.

On an island whose population consists only of knights, who always tell the truth, and liars, who always lie, there is a research institute. Each of its employees once made two statements: a) "There are not even ten people in the institute who work more than I do"; b) "At least one hundred people in the institute get a higher salary than I do." It is known that the workloads of all employees are different, as are their salaries. How many people work in the institute?
Natural numbers $a$, $b$, $x$ and $y$ are such that $ax+by$ is divisible by $a^2+b^2$. Prove that the numbers $x^2+y^2$ and $a^2+b^2$ have a common divisor greater than $1$.

$1994$ volumes of an encyclopedia stand on a shelf. Every morning the librarian Fedya takes three volumes and puts them back in some order in the same places, and every evening the cleaner Dusya swaps some two volumes. Prove that Dusya can act so that at any moment fewer than five volumes stand in their proper places (initially the volumes are arranged by the cleaner).
$H$ is the orthocentre of a triangle $ABC$, and $H_1$ and $H_2$ are its projections onto the bisectors of the interior and exterior angles at $B$. Prove that the line $H_1H_2$ bisects the side $AC$.

A square is divided into several rectangles so that every horizontal line meets exactly $n$ rectangles and every vertical line meets exactly $m$ rectangles (only lines not containing sides of rectangles are considered). What is the smallest possible number of rectangles in the partition?

A finite sequence of numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ is given. For any $k<n$ it is allowed to replace the numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$ inside the sequence by the numbers $$a_{k+1}-a_k,\ a_{k+1}-a_{k-1},\ \ldots,\ a_{k+1}-a_1$$ (in this order). Prove that by such operations one can obtain exactly one sequence in which every number except the last is not less than the half-sum of its neighbours.
The altitudes $BD$ and $AE$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at a point $P$. Prove that $$AB^2=AP\cdot AE+BP\cdot BD.$$
Natural numbers $x$ and $y$ greater than $1$ are such that $x^2+y^2-1$ is divisible by $x+y-1$. Prove that $x+y-1$ is a composite number.
Prove that for all positive real $a$ and $b$ the inequality $a^a+b^b>ab$ holds.

$1994$ points coloured in $10$ colours are placed around a circle. It is known that among any $100$ consecutive points there are points of all colours. Prove that among some $90$ consecutive points there are also points of all colours.
Real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that the numbers $\dfrac{1+bc}{b-c}$, $\dfrac{1+ca}{c-a}$, $\dfrac{1+ab}{a-b}$ are integers. Prove that these integers are pairwise coprime.
Prove that the area of a quadrilateral with sides $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ does not exceed $\frac14\left((a+c)^2+bd\right)$.
Let $a_n$ be the $(n+1)$-th digit from the end of the decimal representation of the number $2^{5^n}$. Prove that the sequence $(a_n)$ is not periodic.

Chuk and Gek play the following game. Gek draws a system of points in the plane, some of which he joins by non-intersecting segments so that the segments do not form closed broken lines. Then, with each move, a player may colour any not yet coloured point in one of $4$ given colours so that no two "neighbouring" points (points joined by a segment) have the same colour. Chuk moves first, and he wins if at the end of the game all points are coloured. Otherwise (if there are no more moves but not all points are coloured) Gek wins. Who wins with correct play?

$1995$ recruits stand in a line. According to the regulations, either every third or every fourth recruit may be sent on latrine-cleaning duty (that is, the first, fourth, seventh, etc., or the first, fifth, ninth, etc.). A detail once formed immediately sets to work. The sergeant-major is going to form three details. Prove that at least one recruit can be sure that he will not get into any of the details.

$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are natural numbers and $N$ is their product. It is known that $N$ is divisible by the square of each of the numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_n$. For each pair $(i,j)$, $i<j$, the greatest common divisor of $a_i$ and $a_j$ was computed; $M$ is the product of all these greatest common divisors. Prove that $M^2$ is divisible by $N$.
A point $O$ is chosen inside a parallelogram $ABCD$ so that $\angle OAD=\angle OCD$. Prove that $\angle OBC=\angle ODC$.

The chess piece "machine-gunner" attacks in one fixed direction along a column or a row (for example, to the left along the row) any number of squares. What is the largest number of machine-gunners not attacking each other that can be placed on a $20\times 20$ board?
$f(x)$ is a polynomial of degree three. Prove that there exists $k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that the polynomial $$f(x)+f(x+1)+\ldots+f(x+k)$$ has exactly one real root.

A circle is circumscribed about an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The altitudes of the triangle from the vertices $A$ and $C$ meet the circle at points $E$ and $F$ respectively, $D$ is an arbitrary point of the (smaller) arc $AC$, $K$ is the intersection point of $DF$ and $AB$, and $L$ is the intersection point of $DE$ and $BC$. Prove that the line $KL$ passes through the orthocentre of the triangle $ABC$.
Prove that in every company consisting of an even number of people there are two people who have an even number of common acquaintances in this company.

A triangle $ABC$ is given. Points $B_1$, $C_1$, $A_1$ are chosen on the extension of the side $AB$ beyond $B$, on the extension of $BC$ beyond $C$ and on the extension of the side $CA$ beyond $A$ respectively, so that $$AB=BB_1,\quad BC=CC_1,\quad CA=AA_1.$$ It turned out that the triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is equilateral. Prove that the triangle $ABC$ is also equilateral.
$a, b, c, d>0$. Prove the inequality $$(ac+bd)^5+(ad+bc)^5\leqslant(a+b)^5(c^5+d^5).$$
Can the numbers from $1$ to $25$ be arranged around a circle so that the sum of any five consecutive numbers leaves remainder $1$ or $4$ upon division by $5$?

$1995$ little people (korotyshki) live in Flower Town. They have $995$ ten-kopeck coins and an unlimited supply of five-kopeck coins. Sometimes the little people exchange coins: one gives another a ten-kopeck coin and receives two five-kopeck coins from him. One evening each of the little people declared: "Today I gave away exactly $10$ coins." Prove that someone was mistaken.

$M$ is a set of primes with more than one element. It is known that for every (finite) subset $N\subset M$ the number $\left(\prod_{k\in N}k\right)-1$ has prime divisors only from $M$. Prove that $M$ coincides with the set of all primes.

The altitudes $AA_1$ and $BB_1$ are drawn in an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. A point $L$ is chosen on the (smaller) arc $AB$ of the circumcircle of the triangle such that $LC=CB$. It turned out that $\angle BLB_1=90^\circ$. Prove that the altitude $AA_1$ is bisected by the altitude $BB_1$.

North Balbesia has $100$ towns, some of which are joined by roads so that one can get from each town to any other. There are $1000$ roads in North Balbesia in all. The government wants to close some roads (possibly all of them) so that an even number of the remaining roads (possibly none) leaves each town. In how many ways can it do this?
Seryozha was solving the equation $f(19x-96/x)=0$ and found $11$ distinct roots. Prove that if he tries hard, he will be able to find at least one more root.

The numbers from $1$ to $2n$ are divided into two groups of $n$ numbers each. Prove that the sets of remainders upon division by $2n$ of the pairwise sums of the numbers of each group coincide (the pairwise sums include expressions of the form $a+a$).

No three diagonals of a convex $1996$-gon pass through one point. Prove that the number of triangles whose vertices lie strictly inside this $1996$-gon and whose sides lie on its diagonals is divisible by $11$ (these are not necessarily triangles of the subdivision; the triangles in question may be divided by diagonals into smaller parts).

Points $A'$ and $C'$ are taken on the diagonal $BD$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ so that $AA'\parallel CC'$. A point $K$ belongs to the segment $A'C$, and the line $AK$ meets the line $C'C$ at a point $L$. A line parallel to $BC$ is drawn through the point $K$, and a line parallel to $BD$ is drawn through the point $C$. These two lines meet at a point $M$. Prove that the points $D$, $M$, $L$ lie on one line.

Find all quadruples of non-constant polynomials $p_1(x), p_2(x), p_3(x), p_4(x)$ with real coefficients having the following remarkable property: for all integers $x, y, z, t$ related by $xy-zt=1$, the equality $$p_1(x)p_2(y)-p_3(z)p_4(t)=1$$ holds.

$M$ is the intersection point of the diagonals of a trapezoid $ABCD$. A point $P$ is chosen on the base $BC$ such that $\angle APM=\angle DPM$. Prove that the distance from the point $C$ to the line $AP$ equals the distance from the point $B$ to the line $DP$.

Two people play the following game on a $100\times 100$ board: the first player marks some free cell of the board, after which the second player puts a domino (a $1\times 2$ rectangle) on the board so that it covers two free cells, one of which is the marked one. The first player wins if the whole board gets covered with dominoes, and the second if not. Who wins with correct play?

Real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{n+1}$; $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ satisfy $$0\leqslant b_k\leqslant 1\ (k=1,\ldots,n)\quad\text{and}\quad a_1\geqslant a_2\geqslant\ldots\geqslant a_{n+1}=0.$$ Prove the inequality (square brackets denote the integer part) $$\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_kb_k\leqslant\sum_{k=1}^{\left[\sum_{m=1}^{n}b_m\right]+1}a_k.$$

Segments $AE$ and $CF$ of equal length are laid off on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. The circle through the points $B$, $C$, $E$ and the circle through the points $A$, $B$, $F$ meet at points $B$ and $D$. Prove that the line $BD$ is the bisector of the angle $ABC$.
Prove that there are no natural numbers $a$ and $b$ such that for any distinct primes $p$ and $q$ greater than $1000$ the number $ap+bq$ is also prime.

A Young diagram is a figure obtained by cutting out of a rectangle, along the grid lines, several rectangular parts whose lower right corners coincide with the lower right corner of this rectangle. A hook is a part of a Young diagram consisting of some cell and all the cells lying either to the right of it or below it. A Young diagram of $n$ cells is given. Let $s$ be the number of hooks consisting of exactly $k$ cells. Prove that $s(k+s)\leqslant 2n$.
