In a triangle $ABC$ the angle $A$ equals $60^\circ$. Inside the triangle there is a point $O$ from which all sides are seen at angles of $120^\circ$. A point $D$ is chosen on the ray $CO$ such that the triangle $AOD$ is equilateral. The perpendicular bisector of the segment $AO$ meets the line $BC$ at a point $Q$. Prove that the line $OQ$ bisects the segment $BD$.

The town N. has $120$ metro lines, and from any station one can get to any other with at most $15$ changes. Two stations are said to be far from each other if at least $5$ changes are needed to get from one to the other. What is the largest number of pairwise far stations that can exist in this town?

$a$, $b$, $c$ are integers such that the polynomial $x^3+ax^2+bx+c$ has three distinct pairwise coprime natural roots and the polynomial $ax^2+bx+c$ has a natural root. Prove that the number $|a|$ is composite.

The natural numbers from $1$ to $n^2$ are placed in the cells of an $n\times n$ table. After placing each number in a free cell, one writes on the board the sum of the numbers already placed in the row and the column containing this cell. When the whole table is filled, the sum of the numbers written on the board is computed. Give an example of a way of placing the numbers for which this sum takes the smallest possible value.

Trees of equal height grow on the equator of the planet Tranai. If all of them fall to the west, the total length of the parts of the equator covered by trees is $100$ km. Prove that if all the trees fall to the east, the total length of the covered parts of the equator is also $100$ km. (The height of the trees is much smaller than the size of the planet.)
The numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy the equations $$x^3-3x^2+5x-17=0\quad\text{and}\quad y^3-3y^2+5y+11=0.$$ Find the value of the expression $x+y$.

The bisector of the angle $A$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ meets the lines $BC$ and $CD$ at points $X$ and $Y$. The point $A'$ is symmetric to the point $A$ with respect to the line $BD$. Prove that the points $C$, $X$, $Y$ and $A'$ lie on one circle.
The sequence of natural numbers $\{x_n\}$ is defined by $$x_1=2,\qquad x_{n+1}=2x_n^2-1.$$ Prove that for all $n$ the numbers $x_n$ and $n$ are coprime.

A computer is programmed to perform the operation: add to a natural number the product of its digits increased by two. The initial number is ten-digit and is chosen at random. Prove that after repeated application of this operation one cannot obtain a $1997$-digit number whose decimal representation consists only of sevens.
Can the cells of a $123\times 456$ table be coloured in two colours so that each cell has exactly two side-neighbouring cells of the other colour?

$1000$ ruffs live in a pond. Each weighs at least a quarter of a pound. Any two ruffs have different numbers of spines. Prove that one can catch at least $220$ pounds of ruffs in such a way that the total weight in pounds of any two caught ruffs is at most the difference of the numbers of their spines.
Can a $75\times 75$ board be divided into pieces of the following two shapes: dominoes ($1\times 2$ rectangles) and five-cell crosses (a cell together with its four side neighbours)?
Prove that for $x\geqslant 2$, $y\geqslant 2$, $z\geqslant 2$ $$(y^3+x)(z^3+y)(x^3+z)\geqslant 125xyz.$$

Circles $S_1$ and $S_2$ meet at points $A$ and $B$. A point $Q$ is chosen on the circle $S_1$. The lines $QA$ and $QB$ meet the circle $S_2$ at points $C$ and $D$, and the tangents to $S_1$ at the points $A$ and $B$ meet at a point $P$. The point $Q$ lies outside $S_2$, and the points $C$ and $D$ lie outside $S_1$. Prove that the line $QP$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $CD$.
A convex $50$-gon with vertices at lattice points is drawn on squared paper. What is the largest number of diagonals of this $50$-gon that can go along grid lines?

The number $99\ldots99$ ($1997$ nines) is written on the board. Once a second one of the numbers written on the board is factored into two factors, after which the number itself is erased and these two factors, each increased or decreased by $2$ (independently of each other), are written instead. Can it happen that eventually the board contains only the number $9$, written several times?

A device consists of $4n$ microchips, every two of which are connected directly by either a red or a blue wire, there being equally many red and blue wires. The device fails completely if one removes some two wires of the same colour joining four (distinct) microchips. An agent of a potential adversary counted the number of ways to disable this device by pulling out two blue wires. Prove that there are exactly as many ways to break it by pulling out two red wires.

Prove that the set of all twelve-digit numbers cannot be split into groups of $4$ numbers so that in each group the numbers coincide in $11$ digits and contain four consecutive digits in the remaining position.

The Aztec diamond of rank $n$ is the figure consisting of the cells of the coordinate grid plane that are entirely contained in the square $\{(x,y)\colon |x|+|y|\leqslant n+1\}$. For an arbitrary tiling of the diamond by $1\times 2$ rectangles (dominoes) the following operation ("switch") is allowed: choose a $2\times 2$ square covered by exactly two dominoes and rotate it by $90^\circ$. Prove that from any tiling one can obtain, in at most $n(n+1)(2n+1)/6$ operations, the tiling consisting only of horizontal dominoes.
Find all positive solutions of the equation $$\max(a,b)\max(c,1998)=\min(a,c)\min(b,1998).$$
A natural number $n$ is such that $n+1$ is divisible by $[\sqrt{n}\,]+1$. Prove that $(n-1)(n-3)$ is divisible by $[\sqrt n\,]-1$.

A city lies on several islands connected by bridges. When travelling around the city, the inhabitants measure the length of their route by the number of bridges they have to cross. After one of the bridges was closed for repair, every citizen declared: "I have a friend to whom the shortest route now contains one bridge more than before." Prove that at least one of the islands is uninhabited.
Two planes divide a cube into four parts of equal volume. Prove that they also divide its surface into four parts of equal area.
Prove that for every natural $n$ the inequality $$\left(1+\frac1n\right)\left(2+\frac1n\right)\cdots\left(n+\frac1n\right)\leqslant 2\cdot n!$$ holds.

Integers are placed in the cells of an $8\times 8$ square. Each cell is covered by a card on which the sum of the numbers in the $3\times 3$ square centred at this cell is written. What is the largest number of numbers in the cells of the square that can certainly be determined if only the numbers on the cards are known?

The following may be done with a sequence of numbers $(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$: choose an arbitrary index $k$, $1\leqslant k\leqslant n$, and replace the number $a_k$ in the sequence by $-(a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n)-k$. How many different sequences can be obtained by such transformations from the sequence $(0,0,\ldots,0)$?

There are $666$ matches in a pile. Two players move alternately. On each move a player may either take from $1$ to $5$ matches from the pile or exchange with the referee $5$ previously taken matches for a toffee. The player who takes the last match wins. Who wins with correct play?

A circle passing through the vertices $A$ and $C$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets the side $AB$ at its midpoint $D$ and the side $BC$ at a point $E$. The circle passing through the point $E$ and tangent to the line $AC$ at the point $C$ meets the line $DE$ at a point $F$. $K$ is the intersection point of the lines $AC$ and $DE$. Prove that the lines $CF$, $AE$ and $BK$ pass through one point.

Can one mark $64$ cells in an $8\times 8\times 8$ "cellular" cube so that every layer of unit cubes parallel to a face contains exactly $8$ marked cells, while among any $8$ marked cells some two necessarily lie in one such layer?
Find all polynomials $P(x,y)$ in two variables such that $P(x+y,y-x)=P(x,y)$ for all $x$ and $y$.

A $2n$-gon $A_1A_2\ldots A_{2n}$ is inscribed in a circle with centre $O$ and radius $1$. Prove that $$\left|\overrightarrow{A_1A_2}+\overrightarrow{A_3A_4}+\cdots+\overrightarrow{A_{2n-1}A_{2n}}\right|\leqslant 2\sin\left(\frac12\left(\angle A_1OA_2+\ldots+\angle A_{2n-1}OA_{2n}\right)\right),$$ where $\angle A_{2k-1}OA_{2k}$ denotes the angular measure of the arc $A_{2k-1}A_{2k}$.
Let $d(n)$ denote the number of natural divisors of $n$. Prove that the sequence $d(n^2+1)$ does not become strictly monotonic from any point on.
There are $169$ people in a squad. Every day four of them go on duty. Can it happen after some time that every two of them have been on duty together exactly once?

Can the letters P, A, S be placed in the cells of an $11\times 11$ table so that the top row reads "PAPASPASPSA", none of the other cells adjacent to the border contains the letter S, and no figure of either of the two shapes shown in the source (an L-shaped piece of three cells consisting of a $2\times 2$ square without its upper right cell, or a $2\times 2$ square without its lower left cell) contains three different letters?
Find the largest value of the expression $$\sqrt[4]{1-a}-\sqrt[4]{a}+\sqrt[4]{a+1}.$$

In a sequence of natural numbers each term, starting with the third, equals either the sum or the absolute value of the difference of the two preceding terms. The first $1999$ terms of this sequence are written on the board. Prove that the sequence can be continued according to this rule so that these $1999$ numbers occur in it again consecutively (in the same order).
The diagonals of a hexagonal cross-section of a cube pass through one point. Prove that the cross-section passes through the centre of the cube.

Traffic lights are placed along a straight highway; on each of them red light is on for one minute and green light for one minute, alternately (not necessarily synchronously). Two cars drive along the highway in the same direction at $60$ km/h. At a red light a car stops instantly, and at a green light it instantly resumes moving at the same speed. Prove that if initially the distance between the cars is greater than $2$ km, then they will never meet.

$AB$ is the shortest side of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the sides $BC$ and $AC$ respectively. Prove that the length of the broken line $AXYB$ is at least twice the length of $AB$.

Several checkers stand on the cells of an infinite board. It is allowed to move any checker to the cell symmetric to it with respect to some other checker; several checkers may stand on the same cell. In positions $A$ and $B$ all checkers stand on different cells not lying on one line, and $B$ can be obtained from $A$ by these operations. Prove that this can be done so that in the intermediate positions all checkers also stand on different cells.
Prove that for $k>2$ the number $2^{2^k-1}-2^k-1$ is composite.

Red, blue and green balloons fly under the dome of a circus, $150$ of each colour. Inside each blue balloon there are exactly $13$ green ones, and inside each red balloon exactly $5$ blue and exactly $19$ green ones. Prove that some green balloon is not contained in any of the other $449$ balloons.

The quadratic trinomial $f(x)=x^2+ax+b$ with integer coefficients has value at $0$ of absolute value at most $800$. It is also known that $f(120)$ is a prime number. Prove that it has no integer roots.

$(a_n)$ is an arithmetic progression consisting of natural numbers, and $p_n$ is the largest prime divisor of $a_n$ for each natural $n$. Prove that the sequence $\left\{\dfrac{a_n}{p_n}\right\}$ is unbounded.

All natural numbers from $1$ to $100$ are written (each once) on the two sides of $50$ cards. The cards lie on the table so that only the numbers on top are visible. Vasya may choose several cards and turn them over simultaneously, and then add up all $50$ numbers that are then on top. What is the largest $S$ for which Vasya can surely obtain a sum not less than $S$?

Two people play the following game. They take turns writing on the board divisors of the number $100!$ (other than $1$, without repetitions). The player after whose move the numbers written on the board are coprime as a whole (have no common divisor greater than $1$) loses. Who wins with correct play: the first player or his opponent?

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle $S$ with centre $O$. The bisector of the angle $ABD$ meets $AD$ and $S$ at points $K$ and $M$ respectively. The bisector of the angle $CBD$ meets $CD$ and $S$ at points $L$ and $N$ respectively. It is known that the lines $KL$ and $MN$ are parallel. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $MON$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $BD$.

A connected graph $G$ has $500$ vertices, and the degree of every vertex is at most $3$. A colouring of the vertices in black and white is called interesting if more than half of the vertices are white but no two white vertices are joined by an edge. Prove that one can choose several vertices of $G$ so that in every interesting colouring more than half of them are black.

Three magicians perform a trick. They give a spectator a deck of cards with the numbers from $1$ to $2n+1$ ($n>6$). The spectator takes one card and distributes the rest equally (in an arbitrary way) between the first and the second magician. Without communicating, each of them studies his $n$ cards, chooses $2$ of them and, putting them in an (ordered) pile, passes them to the third magician. The third magician looks through the $4$ cards received and announces which card the spectator has. Explain how this trick can be performed.
An equilateral triangle of side $9$ is divided into $81$ equal triangles by segments parallel to its sides. Prove that one cannot cut out of it more than $18$ parallelograms with sides $1$ and $2$.

$O$ is the origin of three-dimensional space. The points $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ have non-negative coordinates. Prove the inequality $$\left|\overrightarrow{OA_1}\right|+\left|\overrightarrow{OA_2}\right|+\ldots+\left|\overrightarrow{OA_n}\right|\leqslant\sqrt3\,\left|\overrightarrow{OA_1}+\overrightarrow{OA_2}+\ldots+\overrightarrow{OA_n}\right|.$$

Every month the forester Yermolai planted a row of $2000$ trees along a fence. On each tree he nailed a plate on which he wrote how many oaks there are among the tree itself and its left and right neighbours. In this way a sequence of $2000$ numbers was obtained. How many different sequences could the forester Yermolai obtain?

The polynomial $F(x)=x^{2000}-x^{1000}+1$ is given. Prove that there do not exist $8002$ distinct natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{8002}$ such that $F(a_i)F(a_j)F(a_k)$ is divisible by $a_ia_ja_k$ for all pairwise distinct $i$, $j$ and $k$.

The altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ are drawn in an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. A point $K$ is taken on the side $BC$ such that $\angle BB_1K=\angle A$, and a point $M$ on the side $AB$ such that $\angle BB_1M=\angle C$; $L$ is the intersection point of the altitude $BB_1$ and the segment $A_1C_1$. Prove that the quadrilateral $B_1KLM$ has an inscribed circle.

What is the largest number of rooks that can be placed on an $n\times n$ chessboard so that each of them attacks an even number of the others? We consider that one rook attacks another if they stand on the same column or row and there are no other rooks between them.

Irrational positive numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are such that for every natural $n$ the identity $$[n\alpha]\cdot[n\beta]=[n\gamma]\cdot[n\delta]$$ holds. Does it follow that the sets $\{\alpha,\beta\}$ and $\{\gamma,\delta\}$ coincide? (Square brackets denote, as usual, the integer part of a number.)

Is there a quadratic trinomial $f$ with positive coefficients such that the equality $[f(x)]=f([x])$ holds for every positive number $x$? (Square brackets denote, as usual, the integer part of a number.)

What is the least number of weighings on a balance with a scale needed to put in order weights of $1, 3, 3^2, \ldots, 3^{26}$ g? (A balance with a scale makes it possible to determine the difference of the weights of the loads on its pans.)
$a$ and $b$ are distinct natural numbers greater than $1$, and $a^2+b-1$ is divisible by $b^2+a-1$. Prove that the number $b^2+a-1$ has at least two distinct prime divisors.

The line $\ell$ is the tangent at $B$ to the circumcircle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The point $K$ is the projection of the orthocentre of the triangle onto the line $\ell$, and the point $L$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$. Prove that the triangle $BKL$ is isosceles.

Two balls fly inside a $1\times 1$ square with unit speeds. They do not interact with each other and bounce off the walls according to the law "the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection". Prove that a spider can descend on its thread from the upper side to the lower side with unit speed so that neither it nor the thread is touched by the balls during the descent.

Prove that for all positive numbers satisfying $x_1\leqslant x_2\leqslant\ldots\leqslant x_n$ the inequality $$\frac{x_1x_2}{x_3}+\frac{x_2x_3}{x_4}+\ldots+\frac{x_{n-1}x_n}{x_1}+\frac{x_nx_1}{x_2}\geqslant x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_n$$ holds.

A convex $n$-gon $P$ bounding an area less than $1$ is given in the plane. For each point $X$ of the plane define $F(X)$ to be the area of the union of all segments joining $X$ with points of the polygon (the area of the convex hull). Prove that the set of points $X$ for which $F(X)=1$ is a convex polygon with at most $2n$ sides.
What is the least number of unit segments that must be erased in a $2000\times 3000$ grid rectangle (erasing boundary segments is forbidden) so that no remaining segments form a smaller rectangle?
Do there exist distinct numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ in $[0,\pi/2]$ such that the six numbers $\sin x$, $\sin y$, $\sin z$, $\cos x$, $\cos y$ and $\cos z$ can be divided into three pairs with equal sums?

There are $2000$ towns in a country and no roads at all. Prove that some towns can be joined by roads so that one road leaves each of two towns, two roads leave each of two other towns, three roads leave each of two further towns, $\ldots$, and $1000$ roads leave each of two towns.

Points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ are the midpoints of the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. Points $E$ and $F$ are marked on the midlines $C_1B_1$ and $A_1B_1$ so that the line $BE$ contains the bisector of the angle $AEB_1$ and the line $BF$ contains the bisector of the angle $CFB_1$. Prove that the angles $BAE$ and $BCF$ are equal.
Prove that for all natural numbers $n>m$ the inequality $$[m,n]+[m+1,n+1]>\frac{2mn}{\sqrt{n-m}}$$ holds, where $[x,y]$ is the least common multiple of the numbers $x$ and $y$.

The point $I$ is the incentre of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, and the point $H$ is its orthocentre. The point $M$ is the midpoint of the smaller arc $AC$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$. It turned out that $MI=MH$. Find the angle $\angle ABC$.
Find all functions $f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ such that $f(x+y+f(y))=f(x)+2y$ for all integers $x$ and $y$.

The rectangles $1\times 20$, $1\times 19$, $\ldots$, $1\times 1$ were cut out of a $20\times 20$ table. Prove that the largest number of $1\times 2$ rectangles that can certainly be cut out of the remaining part of the table equals $85$.

Natural numbers not exceeding $10$ are written in a $10\times 10$ table, and the numbers in any two cells adjacent by a side or a corner are coprime. Prove that some number occurs in the table at least $17$ times.

Do there exist quadratic trinomials $f$ and $g$ with leading coefficients equal to one such that for every integer $n$ the number $f(n)g(n)$ is an integer, while the numbers $f(n)$, $g(n)$ and $f(n)+g(n)$ are not integers?
Prove that there are infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that the largest prime divisor of the number $n^4+1$ is greater than $2n$.

An arbitrary point $M$ is chosen inside an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle AMC+\angle ABC=180^\circ$. The lines $AM$ and $CM$ meet the sides $BC$ and $BA$ at points $D$ and $E$ respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $BDE$ passes through a fixed point (different from $B$) not depending on the choice of the point $M$.

A natural number is written on the board. Two players move alternately, and each, on his move, replaces the number $n$ written on the board by the number $n-1$ or $\left[\frac{n+1}{2}\right]$ (square brackets denote the integer part). The player who is the first to write the number $1$ on the board wins. Who wins with correct play, the first player or his partner, if at the beginning of the game the number on the board is $1\,000\,000$?

Real numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{10}$ from the segment $[0,\pi/2]$ are given, the sum of the squares of whose sines equals $1$. Prove the inequality $$3(\sin x_1+\sin x_2+\ldots+\sin x_{10})\leqslant\cos x_1+\cos x_2+\ldots+\cos x_{10}.$$

A convex $2000$-gon $M$ is given, the largest distance between its vertices being equal to $1$. It is known that the area of every convex $2000$-gon whose largest distance between vertices equals $1$ does not exceed the area of the polygon $M$. Prove that the polygon $M$ has two perpendicular diagonals.

Natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are different from $1$. The sequence $\{x_n\}$ is defined by the initial conditions $x_0=0$ and $x_1=1$ and the relations ($n\in\mathbb{N}$) $$x_{2n}=ax_{2n-1}-x_{2n-2},\qquad x_{2n+1}=bx_{2n}-x_{2n-1}.$$ Prove that for all natural $m$ and $n$ the product $x_{n+m}\cdot x_{n+m-1}\cdot\ldots\cdot x_{n+1}$ is divisible by $x_m\cdot x_{m-1}\cdot\ldots\cdot x_1$.

Three quadratic trinomials with pairwise distinct leading coefficients are given. The graphs of any two of them have exactly one common point. Prove that all three graphs have exactly one common point.

$I$ is the incentre of a triangle $ABC$. A circle passing through $I$ touches the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Prove that the segment $XY$ touches the incircle of the triangle $ABC$.
Positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $x$, $y$, $z$ satisfy $a+x=b+y=c+z=1$. Prove the inequality $$(abc+xyz)\left(\frac{1}{ay}+\frac{1}{bz}+\frac{1}{cx}\right)\geqslant 3.$$

$100$ three-cell L-shaped pieces (corners) and several $1\times 3$ rectangles lie on the squared plane. It is known that from all these pieces, without rotating them, one can assemble some rectangle. The excellent pupil Olya took $96$ corners and, without rotating them, assembled $48$ rectangles $2\times 3$ from them. Prove that from the remaining $4$ corners (also without rotating them) one can assemble two more $2\times 3$ rectangles.

On the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ there is a point $K$ such that $AK=2KC$ and $\angle ABK=2\angle KBC$. $F$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$, and $L$ is the projection of $A$ onto $BK$. Prove that the line $FL$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

A sequence $\{a_n\}$ is defined by the relation $$a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n-1}{2}\ \text{ if } a_n\geqslant 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad a_{n+1}=\frac{2a_n}{1-a_n}\ \text{ if } a_n<1.$$ It is known that $a_0$ is a natural number, $a_n\ne 2$ for $n=1, 2, \ldots, 2001$, and $a_{2002}=2$. Find $a_0$.

A zoo has two two-pan balances for weighing animals. An elephant stands on one pan of the first balance and a camel on one pan of the second. It is known that the elephant and the camel weigh an integer number of kilograms and that their total weight does not exceed $2$ tonnes. A set of weights, each weighing an integer number of kilograms, with total weight $2$ tonnes, was delivered to the zoo. It turned out that whatever the weights of the animals, one can distribute some of the weights over all $4$ pans so that both balances are in equilibrium. What is the least number of weights that could have been delivered to the zoo?

Each cell of a $37\times 5$ table ($37$ rows, $5$ columns) contains a number from $1$ to $10$. In each row the numbers are in non-decreasing order from left to right. On every diagonal line in the down-right direction all numbers are equal. Prove that the table has a row containing $5$ equal numbers.

A line is drawn through the incentre of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ with an inscribed circle. It meets the side $AB$ at a point $X$ and the side $CD$ at a point $Y$, and the angles $\angle AXY$ and $\angle DYX$ are equal. Prove that $AX/BX=CY/DY$.
Consider the sequence $a_n=F_n^n$, where $F_n$ are the Fibonacci numbers ($F_1=F_2=1$, $F_{n+1}=F_n+F_{n-1}$). Is the sequence $$b_n=\sqrt{a_1+\sqrt{a_2+\ldots+\sqrt{a_n}}}$$ bounded?

The secret code of any FBI safe is a natural number from $1$ to $900$. Two spies learned one code each and decided to exchange this information. Having agreed on their actions in advance, they met on a river bank near a pile of $26$ stones. First the first spy threw several stones into the water, then the second, then the first again, and so on, until the stones ran out. After that the spies parted. How could the information have been transmitted? (The spies did not say a word to each other.)
Natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that $2a+1$ and $2b+1$ are coprime. What can the greatest common divisor of the numbers $2^{2a+1}+2^{a+1}+1$ and $2^{2b+1}+2^{b+1}+1$ be?

The incircle of a triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ at points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ respectively. A line $\ell$ perpendicular to the segment $AA_1$ is drawn through the point $A_1$. It meets the line $B_1C_1$ at a point $X$. Prove that the line $BC$ bisects the segment $AX$.

A natural number is written on the board. Dima and Sasha play the following game. On his move Dima names some natural number $x$, and Sasha changes the number written on the board by either adding $x$ to it or subtracting $x$ from it (as he chooses). Dima wants a number equal to some power of a given natural number $k$ (including $k^0=1$) to appear on the board. For which values of $k$ can Dima achieve this regardless of the initial number written on the board?
Find all continuous functions $f\colon(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ such that $f(x)f(y)=f(xy)+f(x/y)$ for all positive $x$ and $y$.
Prove that for positive $x$ the inequality $$4x^{17}+17x^{15}\leqslant 17x^{19}+4$$ holds.

The Pickwick Club had $100$ gentlemen. Mr Pickwick counted how many friends each of the other $99$ gentlemen has among these $99$ and wrote the resulting $99$ numbers on a card in some order. The other gentlemen made similar cards. All $100$ cards have been preserved in the archive to this day. Prove that one can compose a hundred-and-first card on which $100$ numbers are written: the numbers of friends of each of the gentlemen.
A point $L$ inside a triangle $ABC$ on the bisector of the angle $A$ is such that $\angle LBC=\angle LCA=\angle LAB$. Prove that the side lengths of the triangle form a geometric progression.

Denote the number $1000!$ by $N$. Can all natural numbers from $1$ to $N$ be placed around a circle in such an order that, going clockwise, each next number is obtained from the previous one by the following operation: add either $17$ or $28$ to the number, and then possibly subtract $N$ from the result?

A polynomial $f(x)$ with integer coefficients is given. It is known that whenever for natural numbers $a$ and $b$ the numbers $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are coprime, the numbers $a$ and $b$ are also coprime. Prove that either $f(0)=0$, or there is a natural number $d>1$ such that $f(n)$ is divisible by $d$ for all natural $n$.

$ABCD$ is a trapezoid ($BC\parallel AD$), $H$ is the orthocentre of the triangle $ABD$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $AD$. It turned out that $HC$ is perpendicular to $BM$. $X$ is the point on the segment $AB$ such that $HX=HB$. $CX$ meets $BD$ at a point $Y$. Prove that $A$, $X$, $Y$, $D$ lie on one circle.
Is there in three-dimensional space a finite set of lines passing through one point in which every line is perpendicular to at least one hundred other lines of this set?
For which $k$ can the frame of a $k\times k$ grid square divided into unit squares be assembled from pieces consisting of three sides of a unit square?

An angle is divided by rays issuing from its vertex into $2n+1$ equal angles. These angles cut out $2n+1$ segments on some line. Prove that the sum of the lengths of the 1st, 3rd, $\ldots$, $(2n+1)$-th segments is greater than the sum of the lengths of the other segments.

Three natural numbers are written on the board. It is allowed to add another of them to one of them and write the sum on the board, erasing one of the summands (for example, from the triple $8, 9, 10$ one can obtain the triple $8, 19, 10$). Prove that one can achieve that some two of the numbers written on the board are equal.
Can the function $f(x)=2^x+3^x+9^x$ be represented as the sum of a finite number of real periodic functions?
Prove that every infinite subset of the natural numbers contains two elements whose sum has a prime divisor greater than one million.

A country has $2003$ towns. They are joined by two-way roads so that between any two towns there is a unique path, and it passes along at most $8$ roads. A town is called remote if at most $8$ roads leave it. Prove that there is a town joined to at least $8$ remote towns.

In a triangle $ABC$ it turned out that $3AC=AB+BC$. The incircle touches the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $K$ and $L$ respectively. $DK$ and $LE$ are diameters of the incircle. Prove that the intersection points of the lines $AE$ and $CD$ with the line $KL$ are equidistant from the midpoint of $AC$.
$1000n^3$ points are marked in space, $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Prove that there are two triangles with vertices at these points the ratio of whose areas is at least $n$.
Several quadratic trinomials are given, each having two roots. The sum of all these trinomials equals $0$. Prove that among these trinomials there are two whose difference has a root.

$k$ cells are marked in a $100\times 100$ square so that for every cutting of the square along the grid lines into two rectangles, one of the rectangles contains at least $100$ marked cells. For what smallest value of $k$ is this possible?

Points $K$ and $L$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively so that $KB=LC$. The point $X$ is symmetric to $K$ with respect to the midpoint of the side $AC$, and the point $Y$ is symmetric to $L$ with respect to the midpoint of the side $AB$. Prove that the line containing the bisector of the angle $A$ bisects the segment $XY$.
Three primes are such that the product of any two of them is a perfect square increased by $6$. Prove that the sum of these primes is a perfect square increased by $9$.

Points $P$ and $Q$ are marked on the sides $AC$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively. It turned out that $AB=AP=BQ=1$ and that the intersection point of the segments $AQ$ and $BP$ lies on the incircle of the triangle $ABC$. Find the perimeter of $\triangle ABC$.

A sequence of natural numbers $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is such that $a_1=1$, and for $n\geqslant 2$, $a_n$ is the smallest natural number not occurring among the numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1}$ such that $a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n$ is divisible by $n$. Prove that $a_{a_n}=n$.

Every two of $100$ volleyball teams played exactly one match with each other. Prove that the teams can be labelled $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_{100}$ so that $A_1$ beat $A_2$, $A_2$ beat $A_3$, $\ldots$, $A_{99}$ beat $A_{100}$, and $A_1$ beat $A_{100}$.
Some $n$ cells of an $n\times n$ square are coloured. For what largest $k$ is there certainly a grid rectangle of perimeter $k$ containing no coloured cells?
A sequence $(x_n)$ is given such that $x_1>0$ and for every natural $n$, $$x_{n+1}=\frac{n}{x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_n}.$$ Prove that $x_{2004}\leqslant 1$.
Natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that $a^3+b^3$ is divisible by $a^2+ab+b^2$, and the number $a-b$ is prime. Prove that $a^3-b^3$ is a perfect fourth power.

A point $D$ is marked on the arc $AC$ not containing $B$ of the circumcircle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, and a point $E$ on the side $AC$ so that $DE=AE$. On the line through $E$ parallel to $AB$ a point $F$ is marked such that $CF=BF$. Prove that the points $D$, $E$, $C$, $F$ lie on one circle.

$2\,000\,000$ toy cars with numbers from $1$ to $2\,000\,000$ stand in different cells of a $2004\times 2004$ racetrack and are controlled by a big computer. The computer issues commands of the form "Car No. $k$: move $1$ cell to the left (right, down, up)". Having received a command, the car moves to the indicated cell if this cell is free and lies inside the racetrack, and then reports to the computer whether it managed to execute the command. Kostya does not see the racetrack and does not know how the cars are placed. Prove that he can write a sequence of commands such that the results of their execution make it possible to determine the initial arrangement of the cars. (All commands must be written before the execution of the first of them begins.)

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ the points $P$ and $Q$ are the midpoints of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. The line $PQ$ meets the sides $AB$ and $CD$ at points $N$ and $M$ respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles $ANP$, $BNQ$, $CMP$, $DMQ$ pass through one point.
A bipartite graph with $v\geqslant 4$ vertices and no multiple edges is drawn in the plane so that each edge intersects at most one other edge. Prove that this graph has at most $3v-8$ edges.
Natural numbers $a, b, c, d>1$ satisfy $a^{b^{c^d}}=d^{c^{b^a}}$. Prove that $a=d$ and $b=c$.
Do there exist four distinct quadratic trinomials with leading coefficients equal to $1$ such that the sum of any two of them has exactly one root?

A circle passing through the vertices $B$ and $C$ of a right triangle $ABC$ meets the hypotenuse $AC$ at a point $X$. The tangents to this circle at the points $X$ and $B$ meet at a point $Y$. Prove that the point $Y$ lies on the midline of the triangle $ABC$ parallel to the side $BC$ or on its extension.
For how many natural numbers $n$ is the incomplete quotient of the division of $1\,000\,000$ by $n$ greater than the remainder?

The numbers from $1$ to $64$ are placed in an $8\times 8$ square so that in every row the numbers increase from left to right and in every column they increase from top to bottom. Let $A$ be the smallest possible value of the sum of the numbers on one of the diagonals, and $B$ the smallest possible value of the sum of the numbers on the other diagonal. Prove that $A=B$.

Baron Münchhausen shot $15$ ducks while hunting, weighing $50, 51, \ldots, 64$ kg. He knows the weight of each duck. Using a pan balance, the baron is going to prove to the spectators that the first duck weighs $50$ kg, the second $51$ kg, the third $52$ kg, and so on (initially the spectators know absolutely nothing about the weights of the ducks). What is the least number of weights the baron needs if both weights and ducks may be placed on both pans and the number of weighings is unlimited? (The values of the weights are known both to the baron and to the spectators. An unlimited supply of weights of $1, 2, \ldots, 1000$ kg is available.)

The bisector of the angle $A$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets the incircle of this triangle at points $F$ and $L$. The point $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from the point $C$ to this bisector. $K$ is the foot of the perpendicular from the incentre to $BD$. Prove that $F$, $L$, $B$ and $K$ lie on one circle.

A horizontal line is drawn along a grid line on an infinite sheet of squared paper. Can one place real numbers of absolute value at most one in the cells of the upper half-plane so that two conditions hold: (i) in each (infinite) column all numbers are distinct; (ii) the number in any cell not lying on the boundary of the half-plane equals the arithmetic mean of its four neighbours?

Ten distinct numbers are written in a row. It is allowed to swap two adjacent numbers if these numbers have not been swapped before. Prove that if fewer than $45$ such operations have been made, then one more can be made.

A sequence of natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{400}$ satisfies $a_{n+1}=d(a_n)+d(n)$. Prove that this sequence contains at most $210$ primes. (Here $d(n)$ denotes the number of natural divisors of $n$.)

A circle passing through the vertices $A$ and $B$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets the sides $AC$ and $BC$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. The centre of the excircle of the triangle $XYC$ tangent to the side $XY$ lies on the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the segment $XY$ passes through the incentre of the triangle $ABC$.
Prove that the equation $3^k=m^2+n^2+1$ has infinitely many solutions in natural numbers.
Prove that for all positive numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ the inequality $$\left(x^2+\frac34\right)\left(y^2+\frac34\right)\left(z^2+\frac34\right)\geqslant\sqrt{(x+y)(y+z)(x+z)}$$ holds.

A company has at least $10$ people. Among any $10$ of them there are three who pairwise know each other. Prove that there are either $7$ people having no acquaintances at all, or $7$ people such that each of the others knows someone among them.

An arbitrary point $X$ is chosen inside a triangle $ABC$. The rays $AX$, $BX$, $CX$ meet the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ at points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ respectively. The point $A_2$ is symmetric to the point $A_1$ with respect to the midpoint of the side $BC$; the points $B_2$ and $C_2$ are defined similarly. Prove that there is a fixed point $Y$, not depending on the choice of $X$, such that the points $Y$, $A_2$, $B_2$ and $C_2$ lie on one circle.

A one is written at one of the vertices of a regular $n$-gon and zeros at the others. The hooligan Misha simultaneously added to the number at each vertex the number of its clockwise neighbour; then he added to the number at each vertex the number standing one vertex further away clockwise (skipping one vertex); then he added to the number at each vertex the number standing two vertices further away clockwise (skipping two vertices), and so on; finally he added to the number at each vertex the number of its counterclockwise neighbour. After these operations $n-1$ of the written numbers turned out to be equal. What could the number $n$ be?

Kostya cuts into parts a $90\times 90\times 90$ cube composed of unit cubes. Every minute he chooses a part of the largest volume (if there are several such parts, any of them) and cuts it in two by a plane cut running along the faces of the unit cubes of the grid (so all parts are boxes composed of unit cubes). Prove that after an hour the volumes of all parts will be less than half the volume of the original cube.
A prime $p$ is given. Prove that the numbers $1!, 2!, 3!, \ldots, (p-1)!, p!$ give more than $\sqrt{p}$ different remainders modulo $p$.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle $\omega$. The tangents to $\omega$ at the points $A$ and $D$ meet at a point $P$, and the arc $ABCD$ lies outside the triangle $ADP$. On the ray $BA$ there is a point $K$ such that $PK\parallel AC$, and on the ray $CD$ a point $N$ such that $PN\parallel BD$. Prove that the points $B$, $C$, $K$, $N$ lie on one circle.
The square with vertices $(0,0)$, $(0,2006)$, $(2006,2006)$ and $(2006,0)$ is divided into $4000$ triangles. Prove that inside one of them there is a point with integer coordinates.

A polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $n$ ($n\geqslant 3$) has $n$ distinct real roots, the smallest of which equals $0$ and the largest equals $1$. a) Prove that the polynomial $p'(x)$ has a root not less than $1-1/n$. b) Prove that the distance between the largest and the smallest root of $p'(x)$ is at least $\sqrt{1-2/n}$.

A triple of real numbers is called good if the two smaller numbers of the triple differ by at most $1$ (for example, $(1,\sqrt3,4)$ is a good triple, and $(1,3,4)$ is not). In some tetrahedron the edge lengths of every face form a good triple. Prove that the half-sums of the lengths of the pairs of opposite (skew) edges also form a good triple.
Solve in natural numbers the equation $n^3-5n+10=2^k$.
problems.proposer: I. Andreeva, N. Kushpel, F. Bakharev, F. Petrov

problems.problem: A circle with centre $I$ is inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ and touches its sides $BC$, $AC$, $AB$ at points $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$ respectively. On the segment $BC_1$ there is a point $K$ such that $IK=IC$. Prove that the midpoint of $KC$ lies on $A_1C_1$.

A country has $100$ towns. Some pairs of towns are to be joined by two-way air routes so that one can fly from any town to any other, and so that for any four towns $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ with routes $A$–$B$, $B$–$C$, $C$–$D$ there is also a route $A$–$D$. In how many ways can this be done?

$2^n+1$ distinct sets are divided into two categories, "red" and "blue", and there are sets of both kinds. A set that is the symmetric difference of a red set and a blue set is called white (it may or may not belong to the original collection of sets). Prove that there are at least $2^n$ white sets.
problems.proposer: D. von der Flaass, M. Alekseev

problems.problem: A convex $n$-gon $F$ is given. A circle is called semi-inscribed in $F$ if it lies entirely in the polygon $F$ and touches three of its sides. It is known that no four lines containing sides of $F$ touch one circle. Prove that there are exactly $n-2$ semi-inscribed circles.

A finite sequence $f(k)$, $k=1, 2, \ldots, n$, is non-decreasing and takes integer values in the interval $[1,n]$. Prove the inequality $$\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(f(k))\leqslant\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(k)+\frac{n^2}{4}.$$

Distinct primes $p$, $q$ and natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_p$; $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_q$ are given. It is known that the sums $a_i+b_j$ give all possible remainders upon division by $pq$. Prove that the numbers $a_i$ give all possible remainders upon division by $p$.

Each pupil of a class wrote in his notebook a geometric progression consisting of three distinct positive numbers. Let $A$ be the sum of the first terms of all these progressions, $B$ the sum of their second terms, and $C$ the sum of their third terms. Prove that the sequence $A$, $B$, $C$ is not an arithmetic progression.
The square of a natural number contains (in its decimal representation) several ones and one two, and no other digits. Prove that it is divisible by $11$.

A hexagon $ABCDEF$ is inscribed in a circle. It turned out that $AB=BD$ and $CE=EF$. The diagonals $AC$ and $BE$ meet at a point $X$, the diagonals $BE$ and $DF$ at a point $Y$, and the diagonals $BF$ and $AE$ at a point $Z$. Prove that the triangle $XYZ$ is isosceles.

A country has $100$ towns and $199$ roads. (Each road joins two towns, and any two towns are joined by at most one road.) One can get from any town to any other along the roads. Prove that one can close several roads forming a closed route so that one can still get from any town to any other along the remaining roads.

Points $E$ and $F$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ so that $AE=EF$ and $\angle CEF=\angle ABC$. A point $K$ on the segment $EC$ is such that $EK=FC$. Prove that the segment joining the midpoints of the segments $AF$ and $EC$ is half as long as $KF$.

Fedya writes from left to right an infinite sequence of non-zero digits. After writing each digit he factors into primes the natural number obtained up to that moment. Prove that sooner or later one of these prime factors will be greater than $100$.
The sequence $x_n$ is defined by the rule $$x_{n+1}=x_n+\frac{x_n^2}{n(n+1)},$$ where $x_1\in(0,1)$. Prove that this sequence is bounded.

A legislative assembly has $200$ deputies. Journalists of a certain newspaper discovered that for any two deputies who have not yet fought each other, each of the other deputies has either already fought both of them or has fought neither of them. Prove that one can form a committee either of $15$ deputies no two of whom have fought each other yet, or of $15$ deputies any two of whom have already fought each other.
Distinct natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfy the relation $$(a+b)(a+c)=(b+c)^2.$$ Prove that $$(b-c)^2>8(b+c).$$

The natural numbers from $1$ to $2007$ are written in a row. Two players move alternately. The first player may, on his move, rearrange the numbers in the row arbitrarily. The second player may choose three consecutive numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ and replace them by the numbers $b$ and $a+c$. When two numbers remain in the row, the first player pays the second a number of roubles equal to the absolute value of the difference of these numbers. What is the largest income the second player can guarantee himself?

A circle passing through the orthocentre of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ and the vertices $A$ and $C$ meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $X$ and $Y$. Points $Z$ and $T$ are chosen on the side $AC$ so that $ZX=ZY$ and $ZA=TC$. Prove that $BT\perp XY$.

Is there a non-constant rational function of two variables $F(x,y)$ such that for all positive $x$ and $y$ the equality $F(x,y)=F\left(y,\frac{y+1}{x}\right)$ holds? (A rational function is a function that is the ratio of two polynomials.)
Positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ satisfy $(a^3+b^3)^4=c^3+d^3$. Prove the inequality $a^4c+b^4d\geqslant cd$.

A sphere and points $A$ and $B$ outside it are given in space. Consider the set of all points $M$ such that the lines $AM$ and $BM$ are tangent to the sphere. Prove that this set is contained in the union of two planes.

An infinite collection of pairwise non-congruent rectangular boxes with integer edges is given. Prove that one of these boxes can be divided into several smaller ones, each of which is congruent to one of the boxes of the collection.

A $10\,000\times 10\,000$ square is given. What is the least number of cells that must be marked in this square so that every $10\times 10$ square and every horizontal $1\times 100$ strip contains at least one marked cell?
A pentagon $ABCDE$ is circumscribed about a circle $\omega$. The side $BC$ touches $\omega$ at a point $K$. It is known that $AB=BC=CD$. Prove that $\angle EKB=90^\circ$.

$2008$ quadratic trinomials $x^2-a_kx+b_k$, $k=1, 2, \ldots, 2008$, are given, whose coefficients $a_k$ and $b_k$ are all the numbers from $1$ to $4016$, each used once. No two trinomials have a common root. All roots of these trinomials were marked on the real line. Prove that the distance between some two marked points is less than $1/250$.

$100$ natural numbers are placed around a circle, no two of which divide one another. Between every two neighbouring numbers one writes (simultaneously) the result of dividing the left one of them by their greatest common divisor, after which the original $100$ numbers are erased. This operation was repeated several times. What is the largest number of ones that can now stand around the circle?

All faces of a tetrahedron $ABCD$ are acute-angled triangles. The altitudes $AK$ and $AL$ are drawn in the faces $ABC$ and $ABD$ respectively. It turned out that the points $C$, $K$, $L$ and $D$ lie on one circle. Prove that $AB\perp CD$.

What is the largest possible value of the greatest common divisor of the three numbers $ab+1$, $bc+1$ and $ac+1$, if $a$, $b$ and $c$ are distinct natural numbers whose sum does not exceed $3\,000\,000$?

A country has $10\,000$ towns, some of which are joined by roads. Fewer than $100$ roads leave each town. Moreover, every cyclic route containing an odd number of roads passes along at least $101$ roads. Prove that the country can be divided into $100$ groups of $100$ towns so that every road joins towns from different groups.
Let $p(a)$ be the smallest prime divisor of a natural number $a$. Natural numbers $m$ and $n$ greater than $1$ satisfy $m^2+n=p(m)+p(n)^2$. Prove that $m=n$.

A superknight is a chess piece one move of which consists of two steps of an ordinary knight. (In particular, a superknight attacks the square on which it stands.) Several cells of the infinite squared plane are painted blue. The number of cells that can be reached by a knight's move from a blue cell equals $N$. Prove that one can place on the board at most $N/8$ superknights that attack all the blue cells.

Two acute-angled triangles $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C_1$ are given. It is known that the sides $AB$, $BC$ and $AC$ of the first triangle are numerically equal to the angles $C_1$, $A_1$, $B_1$ of the second (measured in radians), and conversely, the sides $A_1B_1$, $B_1C_1$, $C_1A_1$ equal the angles $C$, $A$, $B$. What can the sum of the areas of these triangles be?

The excircles touch the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ at points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. The point $L$ is the midpoint of $PQ$, and the point $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. The points $L_1$ and $L_2$ are symmetric to the point $L$ with respect to the midpoints of the segments $BM$ and $CM$ respectively. Prove that $L_1P=L_2Q$.

Two players take turns writing a sequence of natural numbers on the board. Initially the sequence consists of three terms: $1, 2, 3$. In one move one may append to the sequence one term equal to the sum of the last written term and one of the earlier ones. The player who first obtains a number not less than $1000000$ wins. Who wins with correct play?

A point $K$ is chosen inside an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle AKC=2\angle ABC$ and $AK/KC=(AB/BC)^2$. The points $A_1$ and $C_1$ are the midpoints of the sides $BC$ and $AB$. Prove that the point $K$ lies on the circumcircle of the triangle $A_1BC_1$.
A polynomial of degree $n$ with rational coefficients has $n$ distinct irrational roots forming a geometric progression. What values can the number $n$ take?

Integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$, each not greater than $1$, with positive sum are written on $n$ cards (for example: $1,1,1,0,0,0,-2$). A set of cards is called interesting if the sum of the numbers on these cards equals $1$. For every interesting set we write on the board the number $(k-1)!(n-k)!$, where $k$ is the number of cards in this set. Prove that the sum of the numbers written on the board equals $n!$. (In the example given we write $0!6!$ three times, $1!5!$ nine times, $2!4!$ nine times, $3!3!$ four times, $4!2!$ three times, $5!1!$ three times and $6!0!$ once, which sum to $7!$.)

A quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ with real coefficients is given. Let $M$ be the set of values it takes at even $x$, and $N$ the set of values it takes at odd $x$. Prove that the sets $M$ and $N$ either coincide or are disjoint.
Distinct natural numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ satisfy $\operatorname{lcm}(x,y)-\operatorname{lcm}(x,z)=y-z$. Prove that $y$ and $z$ are divisible by $x$.

The streets of Moscow are several concentric circles (ring roads) and several radial avenues drawn from the centre $O$ to the outermost ring. Crossroads $A$ and $B$ lie on the outer ring. Three friends are going to drive from $A$ to $B$: Dima along the outer ring; Kostya first along the avenue $AO$ and then along the avenue $OB$; Sergei claims that he knows a path shorter than both of these. Prove that he is wrong.
A corner cell was cut out of a $2008\times 2008$ grid square. Is the number of ways to cut the resulting figure into three-cell L-shaped pieces (corners) even or odd?

The diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at a point $E$, and the lines $AD$ and $BC$ at a point $F$. The points $X$ and $Y$ are the midpoints of the sides $AD$ and $BC$ respectively. The point $O$ is the circumcentre of the quadrilateral $ABCD$, and the point $O_1$ is the circumcentre of the triangle $EXY$. Prove that $OF\parallel O_1E$.

In a country some pairs of towns are joined by roads, and at least $2008$ roads leave each town. Each road is painted in one of two colours. Prove that there is a non-self-intersecting cyclic route containing at least $504$ roads, all of the same colour.

Let $f(x)=x^2+x$. A sequence of positive numbers $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{10000}$ is such that $b_1$ is an arbitrary number and $$|b_{n+1}-f(b_n)|\leqslant 0.001\quad\text{for } 1<n<10000.$$ Prove that one can choose a positive number $a_1$ and construct the sequence $a_2=f(a_1)$, $a_3=f(a_2)$, $\ldots$, $a_{10000}=f(a_{9999})$ so that $|a_n-b_n|\leqslant 0.1$ for every natural $n\leqslant 10000$.
Solve in positive numbers the system of equations $x^y=z$, $y^z=x$, $z^x=y$.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($AB=BC$) the midpoints $X$ and $Y$ of the sides $AC$ and $AB$ respectively are marked. The point $Z$ is the foot of the perpendicular from the point $B$ to the line $CY$. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $XYZ$ lies on the line $AC$.

A country has $2009$ towns, and every two of them are joined by a road (not passing through other towns). A businessman and the Ministry of Road Construction play a game. Every morning the businessman privatizes one of the roads, and every evening the Ministry destroys ten roads not yet privatized. Can the businessman, despite the Ministry's intrigues, create a cyclic route of privatized roads passing exactly once through exactly $75$ different towns?

A natural number is given. The largest prime not exceeding it is subtracted from it. The same operation is applied to the result, and so on. A number is called good if after several steps it yields $1$, and bad if it yields zero. Prove that among the numbers from $1$ to $1000000$ the good ones make up at least a quarter but at most a half.

A quadrangular pyramid $SABCD$ is given whose lateral faces are acute-angled triangles whose orthocentres lie in one plane. The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of the base of the pyramid meet at a point $P$. It turned out that $SP$ is the altitude of the pyramid. Prove that $AC\perp BD$.
It is known that the positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy $ab+bc+ac=a+b+c$. Prove that $a+b+c+1\geqslant 4abc$.

$600$ natural numbers from the segment $[1,1000]$ are painted crimson. A segment $[k,n]$ of the natural numbers is called tasty if it contains two crimson numbers with any integer difference from $1$ to $n-k$. Prove that there is a tasty segment $[a,b]$ with $b-a\geqslant 199$.

Two quadratic trinomials $f$ and $g$ are given. At some four points the trinomial $f$ takes the values $2$, $3$, $7$ and $10$, and the trinomial $g$ takes at the first three of these points the values $16$, $15$ and $11$ respectively. Find the value of the trinomial $g$ at the fourth point.

The point $O$ is the circumcentre of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ in which the angle $B$ equals $30^\circ$. The ray $BO$ meets $AC$ at a point $K$. The point $L$ is the midpoint of the arc $OC$ not containing the point $K$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $KOC$. Prove that the points $A$, $B$, $L$, $K$ lie on one circle.
Can a $6\times 7\times 7$ box be assembled from $1\times 1\times 2$ bricks so that there are equally many bricks of each of the three possible directions?

A number $x$ is called far from squares and cubes if for every integer $k$ the inequalities $|x-k^2|>10^6$ and $|x-k^3|>10^6$ hold. Prove that there are infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that the number $2^n$ is far from squares and cubes.

A natural number is written on the board. Every minute the difference between its largest proper divisor and its smallest proper divisor is added to the number on the board, and the result is written on the board instead of the original number. (If the number on the board turns out to be prime, the process stops.) Initially a number greater than $1000$ is written. Prove that sooner or later a number not divisible by $17$ will appear on the board.
In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ the point $M$ is the midpoint of the diagonal $AC$, and $\angle MCB=\angle CMD=\angle MBA=\angle MBC-\angle MDC$. Prove that $AD=DC+AB$.

A secret society has $2011$ members, and each has a bank account (with an integer number of roubles in it, which may be negative). From time to time one of the members transfers $1$ rouble from his account to the account of each of his friends in the society. It is known that by a chain of such transfers they can redistribute the money in the accounts in an arbitrary way. Prove that in this society there are exactly $2010$ pairs of friends.
Real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that among the three equations $$x^3-ax^2+b=0,\qquad x^3-bx^2+c=0,\qquad x^3-cx^2+a=0$$ any two have a common root. Prove that $a=b=c$.

A multi-volume encyclopedia "All about dogs" stands on a shelf in alphabetical order, each volume in its own specially assigned place. Next to each place an instruction is attached prescribing one of four actions: move this volume one or two places to the left or to the right. If all the instructions are carried out simultaneously, the volumes end up in the same places in a different order. The dog expert Dima carries out all the instructions every morning. One day he discovered that the volume "Lapdogs" stands in the place originally occupied by the volume "Dachshunds". Prove that after some time the volume "Pugs" will stand in the original place of the volume "Poodles".

The base of a pyramid $SABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ such that $BC\cdot AD=BD\cdot AC$. It turned out that $\angle ADS=\angle BDS$ and $\angle ACS=\angle BCS$. Prove that the plane $SAB$ is perpendicular to the plane of the base.

Real numbers $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ satisfy $$x_1^2+x_2^2+\ldots+x_n^2\leqslant 1.$$ Prove that there are collections of real numbers $y_1, \ldots, y_n$ and $z_1, \ldots, z_n$ such that $$|y_1|+|y_2|+\ldots+|y_n|\leqslant 1,\qquad\max\left(|z_1|,|z_2|,\ldots,|z_n|\right)\leqslant 1$$ and $x_i=\frac{y_i+z_i}{2}$ for all $i$.

Natural numbers $n$ and $k$ with $n\geqslant k$ are given. A natural number $S$ has at least $n$ natural divisors (including one and the number itself). All divisors of $S$ are written in a row in decreasing order. What is the smallest number of divisors that the $k$-th number in this list can have?

$100$ non-intersecting unit segments parallel to the coordinate axes are drawn in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane. These segments are mirrors (on both sides), reflecting light according to the rule "the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection". (When a ray hits the end of a mirror, it does not change its direction.) From a point lying in the unit disc centred at the origin a ray of light is sent in the direction of the bisector of the first coordinate angle. Prove that this initial point can be chosen so that the ray is reflected by the mirrors at most $150$ times.

Some towns of Russia are joined to some towns of Ukraine by international air routes. The Interstate Council for Migration Assistance is going to introduce one-way traffic on each air route so that after leaving a town one cannot return to it (using other one-way air routes). Prove that the number of ways to do this is not divisible by three.
Find the smallest positive non-integer root of the equation $\sin x=\sin[x]$. Here $[x]$ denotes the largest integer not exceeding $x$. Recall that $\pi=3.1415\ldots$

$40$ young men and $10$ young women study at the faculty of mathematics. Each young woman is friends either with exactly all the young men older than her, or with exactly those who are taller than her. Prove that some two young men have the same set of female friends.
The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the edges $AB$ and $CD$ of a tetrahedron $ABCD$. It turned out that $AN=DM$ and $CM=BN$. Prove that $AC=BD$.
Find all pairs of primes $p$ and $q$ (not necessarily distinct) for which the numbers $2p-1$, $2q-1$ and $2pq-1$ are squares of natural numbers.
Numbers $x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1}\in[0,1]$ are given, with $x_{n+1}=x_1$. Prove that $$\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1-x_ix_{i+1}+x_i^2\right)\geqslant 1.$$

Let $S_c$ and $S_a$ be excircles of a triangle $ABC$ ($S_c$ touches the segment $AB$, and $S_a$ the segment $BC$). A circle $S$ passes through the point $B$, touches the circles $S_a$ and $S_c$ externally and meets the segment $AC$ at points $M$ and $N$. Prove that $\angle ABM=\angle NBC$.

The language of wolves has two letters, F and P, and any finite sequence of them forms a word. A word $Y$ is called a descendant of a word $X$ if $Y$ is obtained from $X$ by deleting some letters (for example, the word FFPF has $8$ descendants: F, P, FF, FP, PF, FFP, FPF, FFF). For a given $n$, determine the largest number of descendants that an $n$-letter word of the language of wolves can have.

Denote by $f(x)$ the function equal to $1$ at every integer $x$ and equal to $0$ at all other $x$. The teacher gave the weak pupil Vasya the task of writing the function $f(x)$ using the letter $x$, integers, the signs of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and the operation of taking the integer part. Help Vasya.

In a country some pairs of towns are joined by roads, and at most $100$ roads leave each town. A set of roads is called ideal if these roads have no common endpoints, but no other road can be added to the set preserving this condition. (In the figure two roads forming an ideal set are shown in bold.) Every day the Ministry of Transport chooses some ideal set of roads and destroys them completely. The ministry builds no new roads. Prove that after at most $199$ such operations there will be no roads left in the country.
