A natural number $N$ is given. The numbers from $N^3$ to $N^3+N$ are written on the board. Among them $a$ numbers were painted red, and some $b$ of the remaining ones blue. It turned out that the sum of the red numbers is divisible by the sum of the blue numbers. Prove that $a$ is divisible by $b$.

Points $C_1$ and $B_1$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ respectively so that the segment $B_1C_1$ is parallel to $BC$. The circle through $A$, $B$ and $B_1$ meets the segment $CC_1$ at a point $L$. It is known that the circumcircle of the triangle $CLB_1$ touches the line $AL$. Prove that $AL\leqslant(AC+AC_1)/2$.

An infinite set $M$ of natural numbers is given. For any two distinct elements $a$ and $b$ of it, at least one of the numbers $a^b-2$ and $a^b+2$ also lies in $M$. Prove that $M$ contains at least one composite number.

A child stands in each cell of an $n\times n$ square. Each of them looks towards one of the side-adjacent cells (nobody looks outside the square) and sees either an ear or the back of the head of the child standing in that cell. What is the smallest number of children that can see an ear?

The point $M$ is the midpoint of the arc $BAC$ of the circumcircle of a triangle $ABC$, $I$ is its incentre, and $L$ is the foot of the bisector $AL$. The line $MI$ meets the circumcircle at a point $K$. The circumcircle of the triangle $AKL$ meets the line $BC$ again at a point $P$. Prove that $\angle AIP=90^\circ$.
The numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy $x^2+y^2=1$ and $20x^3-15x=3$. Find $|20y^3-15y|$.
Natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are greater than $1$. It is known that the numbers $a^2+b$ and $a+b^2$ are prime. Prove that the numbers $ab+1$ and $a+b$ are coprime.

A set of weights contains one weight of each of the masses $1, 3, 5, 7, 9, \ldots$ grams. For a natural number $n>1$, prove that the number of ways to make up $n$ grams with these weights is not greater than the number of ways to make up $n+1$ grams.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. The circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ meets the sides $AD$ and $DC$ at points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. The circumcircle of the triangle $ADC$ meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $S$ and $R$ respectively. It turned out that the quadrilateral $PQRS$ is a parallelogram. Prove that the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is also a parallelogram.

A paper square of side $100$ was cut by $99$ vertical and $99$ horizontal lines, producing $10\,000$ rectangles (not necessarily with integer sides). What is the smallest number of rectangles whose area can be less than or equal to $1$?

In the country of Centumia some pairs of towns are joined by roads, and exactly $100$ roads leave each town. A bundle is a set of $10$ roads leaving the same town. Prove that all roads can be divided into several bundles.

A point $K$ is chosen on the bisector $BL$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle AKC-\angle ABC=90^\circ$. A point $S$ is chosen on the extension of the bisector $BL$ beyond the point $L$ such that $\angle ASC=90^\circ$. The point $T$ is diametrically opposite to the point $K$ on the circumcircle of the triangle $AKC$. Prove that the line $ST$ passes through the midpoint of the arc $ABC$.
In a sequence of integers $(a_n)$ the sum $a_m+a_n$ is divisible by $m+n$ for any distinct $m$ and $n$. Prove that $a_n$ is a multiple of $n$ for every $n$.

A rook standing on the surface of a grid cube attacks the cells lying in the same row as its cell, and also on the continuations of this row across one or even several edges. (The figure shows an example for a $4\times 4\times 4$ cube; the visible cells attacked by the rook are shaded grey.) What is the largest number of rooks not attacking each other that can be placed on the surface of a $50\times 50\times 50$ cube?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/spb_2016_1_p2_fig.png
In a tetrahedron the midpoints of all edges lie on one sphere. Prove that its altitudes pass through one point.
$n>4$ points move around a circle, each with constant speed. For any four of them there is a moment of time when they all meet. Prove that there is a moment when all the points meet.

The incircle of a triangle $ABC$ touches the side $AC$ at a point $D$. The segment $BD$ meets the circle again at a point $E$. Points $F$ and $G$ on the circle are such that $FE\parallel BC$ and $GE\parallel BA$. Prove that the line joining the incentres of the triangles $DEF$ and $DEG$ is perpendicular to the bisector of the angle $B$.

A country has $50$ towns, every two towns are joined by (two-way) air routes, and the prices of all flights are pairwise distinct (for any pair of towns the price of the flight "there" equals the price "back"). There is a tourist in each town. Every evening all the tourists move: rich tourists along the most expensive route, and poor tourists along the cheapest route leaving the corresponding town. After $k$ days it turned out that there is again one tourist in each town, and during this time no tourist visited any town twice. For what largest $k$ is this possible?
For a polynomial $P(x)$ with real coefficients one can find a real number $a>1$ such that for every integer $x$ there is an integer $z$ with $aP(x)=P(z)$. Find all such polynomials $P(x)$.

The pupils of a school attend $m$ circles. Exactly $mk$ children attend each circle. Prove that all the pupils of the school can be distributed among $k$ classrooms so that each classroom contains at least one representative of each circle ($m$ and $k$ are natural numbers).

A circle passing through the vertices $A$ and $B$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets the sides $AC$ and $BC$ at points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. The median from the vertex $C$ bisects the arc $PQ$ of this circle. Prove that the triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.
Numbers $x, y, z, t\in(0,\pi/2]$ satisfy $$\cos^2x+\cos^2y+\cos^2z+\cos^2t=1.$$ What is the smallest value that the quantity $$\cot x+\cot y+\cot z+\cot t$$ can take?

A natural number $n$ is called almost a square if $n$ can be represented in the form $n=ab$, where $a$ and $b$ are natural numbers with $a\leqslant b\leqslant 1.01a$. Prove that for infinitely many natural $m$ none of the numbers $m, m+1, m+2, \ldots, m+198$ is almost a square.

The altitude $PH$ is drawn in a tetrahedron $PABC$. Perpendiculars $HA'$, $HB'$ and $HC'$ are dropped from the point $H$ to the lines $PA$, $PB$ and $PC$. The planes $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ meet along a line $\ell$. The point $O$ is the circumcentre of the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the lines $OH$ and $\ell$ are perpendicular.

In a country some mathematicians know each other, and for every partition of the mathematicians into two non-empty groups there are two acquaintances from different groups. It is known that if any set of $4$ or more mathematicians is seated at a round table so that any two neighbours are acquainted, then there are two acquaintances at the table who do not sit next to each other. Denote by $c_i$ the number of sets of $i$ pairwise acquainted mathematicians. Prove that $c_1-c_2+c_3-c_4+\ldots=1$.

A convex polygon with vertices at integer points containing the origin $O$ inside is given in the plane. Let $V_1$ be the set of vectors from $O$ to the vertices of the polygon, and $V_2$ the set of vectors from $O$ to all integer points contained inside and on the boundary of the polygon (thus $V_1$ is contained in $V_2$). Two grasshoppers jump on integer points: each jump of the first grasshopper shifts it by a vector of the set $V_1$, and of the second by a vector of $V_2$. Prove that for some number $c$ the following holds: if both grasshoppers can jump from $O$ to some point $A$, and the second needs $n$ jumps for this, then the first can do it in at most $n+c$ jumps.

A line $\ell$ in the coordinate plane is not parallel to the coordinate axes. For what smallest $d$ can one assert that the distance from some point with integer coordinates to $\ell$ does not exceed $d$?

Vasya has $100$ cards of three colours, with at most $50$ cards of each colour. Prove that he can lay out a $10\times 10$ square from them so that any two (side-)adjacent cards have different colours.

A point $T$ is chosen on the bisector of the angle $B$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The circle $S$ constructed on $BT$ as a diameter meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. The circle passing through the vertex $A$ and tangent to $S$ at the point $P$ meets the line $AC$ again at a point $X$. The circle passing through the vertex $C$ and tangent to $S$ at the point $Q$ meets the line $AC$ again at a point $Y$. Prove that $TX=TY$.
It is known that the quadratic trinomial $$(b+c)x^2+(a+c)x+(a+b)$$ has no roots. Prove that $4ac-b^2\leqslant 3a(a+b+c)$.

A regular hexagon is divided into equal rhombi with sides parallel to the sides of the hexagon. Directions are assigned to three pairwise non-adjacent sides of the hexagon, following the counterclockwise traversal of the hexagon. Then on each side of each rhombus an arrow is placed directed in the same way as the side of the hexagon parallel to this side. Prove that there is no closed path going along the arrows.
Positive irrational numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are such that for all $x>0$ the equality $[\alpha[\beta x]]=[\beta[\alpha x]]$ holds. Prove that $\alpha=\beta$.
problems.proposer: J. Lagarias, T. Murayama, D. Richman

problems.problem: Points $A$ and $B$ are marked on a circle $S$. The tangents to the circle $S$ at the points $A$ and $B$ meet at a point $C$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the segment $AB$. A circle $S_1$ passing through the points $M$ and $C$ meets the segment $AB$ again at a point $D$, and the circle $S$ at points $K$ and $L$. Prove that the tangents to the circle $S$ at the points $K$ and $L$ meet on the segment $CD$.

A polynomial $f(x)$ of degree $2000$ is given. The polynomial $f(x^2-1)$ has exactly $3400$ roots, and the polynomial $f(1-x^2)$ has exactly $2700$ roots. Prove that the distance between some two roots of $f(x)$ is less than $0.002$.

$100$ distinct natural numbers are written on the board. To each of these numbers the greatest common divisor of all the others was added. Could three of the $100$ numbers obtained as a result be equal?

At the beginning of the game Malysh and Karlsson have one piece of chocolate in the form of a $2019\times 2019$ square of cells. On each move Malysh divides some piece along the grid lines into three rectangular pieces, and Karlsson eats one of these three pieces of his choice. The game ends when the next move is impossible. If the total number of moves made is even, Malysh wins; if it is odd, Karlsson wins. Who wins with correct play?

A scalene triangle $ABC$ of perimeter $12$ is inscribed in a circle $\omega$. The points $P$ and $Q$ are the midpoints of the arcs $ABC$ and $ACB$ respectively. The tangent to the circle $\omega$ at the point $A$ meets the ray $PQ$ at a point $R$. It turned out that the midpoint of the segment $AR$ lies on the line $BC$. Find the length of the segment $BC$.

Baron Münchhausen has a set of weights of $1000$ different integer masses, with $2^{1000}$ weights of each mass. The baron claims that if one takes one weight of each mass, the total mass of these $1000$ weights will be less than $2^{1010}$, and that this mass cannot be made up with weights of this set in any other way. Can the baron's words be true?

Suppose there are roads $AB$ and $CD$ between towns $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$, but no roads $BC$ and $AD$. A reconstruction is the replacement of the pair of roads $AB$ and $CD$ by the pair of roads $BC$ and $AD$. Initially a country had several towns, some pairs of which were joined by roads, with $100$ roads leaving each town. The minister drew a new road map in which $100$ roads still leave each town. It is known that both in the old and in the new map no two towns are joined by more than one road. Prove that the new map can be obtained from the old one by several reconstructions.

A triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle $\omega$ with centre $O$. The line $AO$ meets the circle $\omega$ again at a point $A'$. $M_B$ and $M_C$ are the midpoints of the sides $AC$ and $AB$ respectively. The lines $A'M_B$ and $A'M_C$ meet the circle $\omega$ again at points $B'$ and $C'$, and meet the side $BC$ at points $D_B$ and $D_C$ respectively. The circumcircles of the triangles $CD_BB'$ and $BD_CC'$ meet at points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that the points $O$, $P$ and $Q$ lie on one line.

A natural number is called hypotenusal if it can be represented as the sum of the squares of two non-negative integers. Prove that every natural number greater than $10$ is the difference of two hypotenusal numbers.

A short-sighted rook attacks all cells of its row and its column that can be reached in at most $60$ steps, stepping from a cell to a side-adjacent one. What is the largest number of short-sighted rooks not attacking each other that can be placed in a $100\times 100$ square?

The bisector $BB_1$ is drawn in a scalene triangle $ABC$. The point $I$ is the incentre of the triangle $ABC$. The perpendicular bisector of the segment $AC$ meets the circumcircle of the triangle $AIC$ at points $D$ and $E$. A point $F$ on the segment $B_1C$ is chosen so that $AB_1=CF$. Prove that the points $B$, $D$, $E$ and $F$ lie on one circle.

The sum $$\frac{2}{3\cdot 6}+\frac{2\cdot 5}{3\cdot 6\cdot 9}+\ldots+\frac{2\cdot 5\cdot\ldots\cdot 2015}{3\cdot 6\cdot\ldots\cdot 2019}$$ was written as a decimal fraction. Find the first digit after the decimal point.

The altitudes $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at a point $H$. A circle with centre $O_b$ passes through the points $A$, $C_1$ and the midpoint of the segment $BH$. A circle with centre $O_c$ passes through the points $A$, $B_1$ and the midpoint of the segment $CH$. Prove that $B_1O_b+C_1O_c>\frac{BC}{4}$.

The sequence $a_n$ is defined by the conditions $$a_1=1,\quad a_2=2\quad\text{and}\quad a_{n+2}=a_n(a_{n+1}+1)\ \text{ for } n\geqslant 1.$$ Prove that $a_{a_n}$ is divisible by $(a_n)^n$ for $n\geqslant 100$.

$N$ oligarchs built themselves a country with $N$ towns, each oligarch owning exactly one town. In addition, each oligarch built several roads between towns: any pair of towns is joined by at most one road of each of the oligarchs (two towns may be joined by several roads belonging to different oligarchs). In total $d$ roads were built. Some oligarchs would like to form a corporation, uniting their towns and roads, so that one can get from any town of the corporation to any other of its towns along roads of this corporation, possibly passing through towns of other oligarchs on the way. But it turned out that no group of fewer than $N$ oligarchs can form a corporation! For what largest $d$ is this possible?

A prime $p$ is given. All natural numbers from $1$ to $p$ are written in a row in increasing order. Find all $p$ for which this row can be divided into several blocks of consecutive numbers so that the sums of the numbers in all blocks are equal.

The cells of a $100\times 100$ table are coloured white. In one move it is allowed to choose any $99$ cells of one row or of one column and to recolour each of them in the opposite colour, from white to black and from black to white. What is the least number of moves needed to obtain a table with a chessboard colouring of the cells?

In a pyramid $SA_1A_2\ldots A_n$ all lateral edges are equal. The point $X_1$ is the midpoint of the arc $A_1A_2$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $SA_1A_2$, the point $X_2$ is the midpoint of the arc $A_2A_3$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $SA_2A_3$, and so on, the point $X_n$ is the midpoint of the arc $A_nA_1$ of the circumcircle of the triangle $SA_nA_1$. Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles $X_1A_2X_2$, $X_2A_3X_3$, $\ldots$, $X_nA_1X_1$ pass through one point.

The functions $$F(x)=x^2+\frac{12}{x^2},\qquad G(x)=\sin(\pi x^2)\qquad\text{and}\qquad H(x)=1$$ are written on the board. If functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are already written on the board, one may also write the functions $$f(x)+g(x),\qquad f(x)-g(x),\qquad f(x)g(x),\qquad cf(x)$$ (the last one with any real coefficient $c$). Can a function $h(x)$ appear on the board such that $|h(x)-x|<\frac13$ for all $x\in[1,10]$?
A natural number $n$ is given. For each prime $p$ in the interval $[n,n^2]$ the number $\frac1p$ was computed, and all the numbers obtained were added. Prove that their sum is less than $2$.

The point $M$ is the midpoint of the base $AD$ of a trapezoid $ABCD$ inscribed in a circle $\omega$. The bisector of the angle $ABD$ meets the segment $AM$ at a point $K$. The line $CM$ meets the circle $\omega$ again at a point $N$. Tangents $BP$ and $BQ$ are drawn from the point $B$ to the circumcircle of the triangle $MKN$. Prove that the lines $BK$, $MN$ and $PQ$ pass through one point.

A square is cut into red and blue rectangles. The sum of the areas of the red rectangles equals the sum of the areas of the blue ones. For each blue rectangle we write down the ratio of the length of its vertical side to the length of its horizontal side, and for each red rectangle the ratio of the length of its horizontal side to the length of its vertical side. Find the smallest possible value of the sum of all the numbers written.
Can one mark points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ on the parabola $y=x^2$ and points $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$ on the parabola $y=2x^2$ so that the convex quadrilaterals $ABCD$ and $EFGH$ are congruent?

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ with angle $45^\circ$ at the vertex $A$ the altitudes $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$ are drawn. The ray $EF$ meets the line $BC$ at a point $X$. It turned out that $AX\parallel DE$. Find the angles of the triangle $ABC$.

Ivan and Koschei play the following game. Initially the polynomial $x-1$ is written on the board. In one move one may replace the polynomial $f(x)$ written on the board by the polynomial $$ax^{n+1}-f(-x)-2,$$ where $n$ is the degree of the polynomial $f(x)$ and $a$ is one of its real roots. The players move alternately, Ivan first. The player after whose move the board contains a polynomial having no real roots wins. Can Ivan defeat Koschei?

A collection of numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_m$ is said to be stronger than a collection of numbers $b_1, \ldots, b_n$ if among all inequalities of the form $a_i>b_j$ the number of true inequalities is at least twice the number of false ones. Prove that there are no three collections $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $A$ is stronger than $B$, $B$ is stronger than $C$, and $C$ is stronger than $A$.

The altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at a point $H$. A perpendicular $HQ$ is dropped to the tangent drawn from the point $C$ to the circumcircle of the triangle $AB_1C_1$ (the point $Q$ lies inside the triangle $ABC$). Prove that the circle passing through the point $B_1$ and tangent to the line $AB$ at the point $A$ is also tangent to the line $A_1Q$.

Find all pairs of non-zero (not necessarily positive) rational numbers $x$, $y$ with the following property: every positive rational number can be represented in the form $\{rx\}/\{ry\}$ with a positive rational $r$.

There are $2n$ cards, each bearing a number from $1$ to $n$ (each number on exactly two cards). The cards lie on the table face down. A set of $n$ cards is called good if each number occurs on them exactly once. Baron Münchhausen claims that he can indicate $80$ sets of $n$ cards of which at least one is certainly good. For what largest $n$ can the baron's words be true?
Let $f(x)$ be a quadratic trinomial and $g(x)$ a polynomial of degree $3$. Can the polynomial $f(g(x))$ have six distinct roots that are powers of $2$?

The median $BM$ is drawn in a triangle $ABC$. A point $D$ is marked on the extension of the side $AC$ beyond the point $C$ such that $BD=2CD$. The circumcircle of the triangle $BMC$ meets the segment $BD$ at a point $N$. Prove that $AC+BM>2MN$.

Irreducible fractions $\frac ab$ and $\frac cd$ were written as purely periodic decimal fractions. It turned out that every finite sequence of consecutive digits occurring in the first decimal fraction after the decimal point also occurs in the second one (also consecutively and also after the decimal point). Prove that $b=d$.
What is the least number of operations needed to recolour a white $100\times 100$ board black if in one operation one may recolour in the opposite colour any $99$ cells of any row or any column?

A natural number $a>1$ is given. Define the function $$f(n)=n+\left[a\{n\sqrt2\}\right].$$ Prove that there is a natural $n$ such that $f(f(n))=f(n)$ but $f(n)\ne n$. Recall that $[x]$ is the integer part of $x$, i.e. the largest integer not exceeding $x$, and $\{x\}=x-[x]$ is the fractional part of $x$.

A triangle $ABC$ is given. The point $X$ is symmetric to the vertex $B$ with respect to the line $AC$, and the point $Y$ is symmetric to $C$ with respect to $AB$. The tangent at the point $A$ to the circumcircle of the triangle $XAY$ meets the lines $XY$ and $BC$ at points $E$ and $F$ respectively. Prove that $AE=AF$.

In a connected graph $G$ two disjoint sets of vertices $X$ and $Y$ are given, and there is no edge between these sets. Let the graph $G-X$ have exactly $m$ connected components and the graph $G-Y$ exactly $n$ connected components. What is the smallest possible number of connected components of the graph $G-(X\cup Y)$? Recall that for a set of vertices $W$, $G-W$ denotes the graph obtained from $G$ by deleting all vertices of the set $W$ and all edges issuing from them.

A $100\times 100$ table is filled with the numbers from $1$ to $10\,000$ as shown in the figure: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 1 & 2 & 3 & \ldots & 100\\ \hline 101 & 102 & 103 & \ldots & 200\\ \hline \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \hline 9901 & 9902 & 9903 & \ldots & 10\,000\\ \hline\end{array}$$ Can some numbers be rearranged so that each cell still contains one number and the sum of the numbers in every rectangle of three cells is unchanged?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/spb_2024_1_p1_fig.png

The sequence $a_n$ is given: $$1,\ 2,\ 2,\ 3,\ 3,\ 3,\ 4,\ 4,\ 4,\ 4,\ \ldots$$ (one one, two twos, three threes, and so on), and another sequence $b_n$ such that $a_{b_n}=b_{a_n}$ for all natural $n$. It is known that $b_k=1$ for some $k>100$. Prove that $b_m=1$ for all $m>k$.

In a scalene triangle $ABC$ the bisector $AK$ is drawn. A diameter $XY$ of its circumcircle is perpendicular to the line $AK$ (the order of the points on the circumcircle is $B$–$X$–$A$–$Y$–$C$). A circle passing through the points $X$ and $Y$ meets the segments $BK$ and $CK$ at points $T$ and $Z$ respectively. Prove that if $KZ=KT$, then $XT\perp YZ$.

A $101$-digit number $a$ and an arbitrary natural number $b$ are given. Prove that there is a natural number $c$ with at most $102$ digits such that every number of the form $\overline{caaa\ldots ab}$ is composite.

$100$ points in general position (i.e. no three on one line) are marked in the plane. Prove that one can choose three marked points $A$, $B$, $C$ so that for every point $D$ of the remaining $97$ marked points the lines $AD$ and $CD$ contain no points lying inside the triangle $ABC$.

A polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients is given. For some natural $n$ the numbers $P(0), P(1), \ldots, P(2^n+1)$ are divisible by $2^{2^n}$. Prove that the values of the polynomial $P(x)$ at all integer points are divisible by $2^{2^n}$.

A tourist arrived on an island where $100$ wizards live, each of whom can be a knight or a liar. He knows that at the moment of his arrival one of the hundred wizards is a knight (but does not know which one), and the others are liars. The tourist may choose any two wizards $A$ and $B$ and ask $A$ to cast on $B$ the spell "Vzhukh!", which changes the nature (turns a knight into a liar and a liar into a knight). The wizards fulfil the tourist's requests, but if at that moment wizard $A$ is a knight, then the nature of $B$ really changes, and if $A$ is a liar, it does not change. The tourist wants, after several successive requests, to know simultaneously the nature of at least $k$ wizards. For what largest $k$ can he achieve his goal?

$100$ red and $99$ blue "zhivoglots" were released into the empty Quiet Pool. When a zhivoglot wants to eat, it may eat two other zhivoglots. If its victims are of the same colour, the zhivoglot changes its colour, and if they are of different colours, it does not. In the end only one zhivoglot remained. What is its colour?
Prove that $$\frac{1+\tan 1^\circ}{1-\tan 1^\circ}+\frac{1+\tan 2^\circ}{1-\tan 2^\circ}+\ldots+\frac{1+\tan 15^\circ}{1-\tan 15^\circ}>19.$$

A prime $p$ has the following property: for all integers $a$ and $b$ the sequence defined by the conditions $x_1=a$, $x_2=b$ and $x_{n+2}=x_{n+1}+x_n$ for $n\geqslant 1$ contains a term divisible by $p$. The sequence of Fibonacci numbers is defined by $F_1=F_2=1$ and $F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n$ for $n\geqslant 1$. Prove that $F_{p+1}$ is divisible by $p$.

A point $B$ is fixed on the bisector of an angle with vertex $A$. An arbitrary point $O$ is chosen on the segment $AB$ such that the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OB$ meets the sides of the angle at four points. Join by a segment two of these points lying on different sides of the angle and at different distances from $A$. Prove that all segments constructed in this way are tangent to one fixed circle.
A natural number $m$ is given. Prove that there are infinitely many natural numbers $n$ coprime to $m$ for which the number $(n!)^2+1$ is composite.

A connected graph has more than $1000$ vertices, and it remains connected even if any $100$ vertices are deleted from it. Prove that this graph contains a path $a_1a_2\ldots a_{102}$ such that after deleting these $102$ vertices the graph remains connected. (Some pairs of non-consecutive vertices of the path may also be adjacent.)

A collection of numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{10}$ is called good if $$|x_{i+1}-x_1|\geqslant 3|x_i-x_1|\quad\text{for } i=1, 2, \ldots, 9.$$ Prove that from any $314\,159$ real numbers one can choose a good collection.

A set of cells on a rectangular board is called a histogram if together with any cell it contains all cells of the same column lying below it. Prove that if in a histogram the numbers of cells in any two neighbouring columns are either equal or differ by a factor of $12$, and the total number of cells of the histogram is divisible by $11$, then this histogram can be cut into $1\times 11$ rectangles (the rectangles may be rotated).
It is known that $x\cdot 2^y=y\cdot 2^x=1$. Prove that $x=y$.
The last non-zero digits of the numbers $1^1, 2^2, 3^3, \ldots$ are written on the board from left to right. Prove that this sequence is not periodic from any point on.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the sides $AD$ and $CD$ such that $\angle A=\angle C=\frac12\angle PBQ$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ so that $DX\parallel BQ$ and $DY\parallel BP$. Prove that if the quadrilateral $APQC$ is cyclic, then the quadrilateral $AXYC$ is also cyclic.

An $n$-element set $X$ is given, where $n>1$. A collection of its subsets is called generating if any subset of the set $X$ can be obtained from them by means of intersections and unions. Two sets are written on the board: $\varnothing$ and $X$. Two players take turns writing subsets of the set $X$ on the board (all sets on the board must be distinct). The player after whose move the subsets on the board form a generating collection wins. Who wins with correct play: the first player or his opponent?

$n>1$ lines in general position are drawn in the plane, dividing the plane into several regions (some of them unbounded). Each of these lines is divided by the other lines into $n$ intervals (segments and rays). Prove that numbers from the set $\{-1,-2,-3,1,2,3\}$ can be placed on all these intervals so that the sum of the numbers on the boundary of every region equals zero.
Is it true that for every natural $N$ there are natural numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $$\gcd(a^4+15,\,b^4+15)>(a-b)^5>N?$$
